核心难题：AI 写得了代码，但能理解"运行时"吗？

Martin: One question I always have: I can understand why these models can generate code — they're trained on all the code ever written. That's the syntax piece.

But for core infrastructure, distributed algorithms, the properties — how it handles itself when it's running — are very different. Often you can't even look at the syntax to know what's going to happen. Say you're writing some distributed system — the performance, the availability, the correctness, is going to depend on what the workload looks like, what the access patterns are, what the traffic is.

Jad: Are you talking about performance aspects, or…?

Martin: Availability — you may have to lock things so they're not available for a period. Correctness — maybe you've decided to do eventual consistency, so if you do a read it's not going to be consistent because there isn't a lock. Performance — maybe you cache, maybe you don't. These are trade-offs in the design space. Unless you know the access patterns, you won't know how it's going to perform.

I can understand how an AI will write code for a generic distributed data store. What I don't understand is how it will know to make the trade-offs needed — because it doesn't even know what the access patterns are. And where's even the data to learn how to build a system that understands all of the operations? Today we rely on human beings to manage clusters, optimize databases, etc.

Can you talk about how you think of this? I get the writing-the-code part, but with these deep operational systems — how do you apply AI? Have we made any progress at all, or is this still an outstanding problem?

Jad: The question is maybe about complexity, and to what extent can you take the things you've described that are operational, that happen in production, and convert them into something an AI can reason about.

Martin: First — how often does it get it right? Performance, correctness? How good a job does it do? And second — how do we make it reason about that? If I use the Jad method, how often does what it writes actually run operationally sensibly?

I'll tell you — I work on this distributed Gaussian splat renderer, and it's bad. Horrible. You've got millions of Gaussian splats you've got to page in and out and stream, and it just totally depends on the running system. None of the models do a good job.

Jad: In our world, we've defined really well what performance benchmarks look like and how the system should run, and what the constraints of actually building within our stream processor look like.

But every once in a while — my latest project has been all about query optimization and query performance. I was like: "We are basically generating code that corresponds to SQL and we want to run it in a pipeline." I said, "You're generating bad code — fix it."

Initially it wasn't doing any optimization on the code. "It's fine, looks like, what's the problem?" I said, "Look, there are these conjuncts you're doing, this particular term is repeated and should have been taken away." It went on a thread to figure out all the things it could optimize to make this better. Ultimately it was able to do a relatively good job — because it could ground that in performance benchmarks. I said, "Here's a dataset of the queries and what the users are asking. Go work on it."

But when it comes to saying something like: "How much memory should I give this system?" — it has no idea. That has to come from actual experiments that run in production.

What these systems seem to be doing well at this point in operational stuff is: it knows that "I probably won't be able to answer this question — let me run an experiment and come up with that information." Of course, when it comes to operations, production systems don't behave the way you expect — and ultimately, that's why incidents happen.

AIOps 的翻转：不要回溯根因，先探测"变化"

Martin: Have you found — are you doing any of the AIOps stuff where you have a running system that has logs, you feed it to an AI, and that helps you tweak it? And how well does that work? Because anecdotally my experience with other people doing this has not been great.

Jad: We're doing it for both operational pieces and security, but the way we're tackling it is not the way other people are doing it.

A lot of those AIOps systems basically start from a lagging indicator — "hey, this metric spiked" or "this alert happened" — go back through a very complex system and try to determine why that happened. That's why those don't work — because backtracking into a root cause is actually very problematic.

Instead, what we're doing is the other way around: can we actually start by figuring out if there's something different in your environment that has changed? Can we do large-scale clustering, find a needle in a haystack — something that is different?

Martin: So you're assuming it was working fine before and now it's not. Something happened — but it could just be a change in normal traffic patterns.

Jad: That's fine too. The thing we're looking at: when things go wrong, usually the system will tell you something went wrong somehow. If it's working fine and scaling as normal, nothing will happen. But sometimes you'll see some message that says "error connections ran out," or "memory exceeded," or "resource buffer is emptied" — some early warning. That's the one message we want to capture, and then go from there and see: is that an actual problem we need to investigate?

Martin: How does it do?

Jad: So far it's doing pretty well. We're running it internally in our systems. We ran it in a couple of our customers' environments, and in the couple of cases where we ignored it — those turned into production incidents.

Martin: Really? Oh wow.

真正的哲学分歧：操作系统的状态空间是否可学习？

Martin: From an intuitive perspective, I can understand how these models understand syntax — they're trained on all the code ever written, and that covers a lot of useful cases. It's hard for me to even think of a bound on the actual operations of software. It's a ridiculous statement but kind of true: every time you add a bit to a program, the state space of what it can do operationally increases by a factor of two. You very quickly get to more states than atoms in the universe.

Arguably, this is why product approaches to operations have never really worked. Chaos engineering never really worked. We've always relied — the dirty secret for the longest time of running a distributed cluster — on human beings managing it. And to train an AI to do it, you have to have enough data and enough configurations.

Do you think we're at a spot where you could use AI to run a distributed cluster or run one of these services, or do you think that's still on the come?

Jad: I think there's enough to have it start that loop. Ultimately — I agree with you, there's infinite space, a lot of different things — but humans also operate on runbooks. Sure, there's a lot that happens in production where you need some human to go and like, "Hey, this is too complex, there's some state that's hidden that I know of because I talked to this other guy at the water fountain the other day." A lot of stuff isn't visible in the state of the system.

But I'd argue the goal is to get enough telemetry and enough understanding to make everything really visible. And then most of the issues that end up really showing up in operations — assuming you have the system previously running okay — is due to some kind of change. If you're able to focus on figuring out what the change was —

Martin: Can I ask a stupid question? I never think of these generative models as that good at predicting stuff — and it sounds like you're talking a lot about predictive modeling. You predict a change, or you baseline and detect an anomaly. Am I thinking about this wrong?

Jad: No, you're not. The goal is not actually having the agent try to predict, but have it get a signal that something changed.

Martin: Deterministically.

Jad: Yes.

Martin: Wait — so there is a separate model that does the predictive stuff, and then that will alert the AI?

Jad: Yes. What we do is: you give us your petabyte of logs per day, and we scan all of them. Every time we see a new kind of pattern emerge in your logs — a new thing we haven't seen before — we lift it up to the AI.

Martin: I see. So that's a predictive model that does what predictor models are good at — determining out-of-norm things. That goes to the AI, and the AI uses that to figure out what to do.

Jad: Exactly. The AI can then reason and drive that down. It can say, "Oh, this message — let me actually look at the code and figure out where it comes from, understand what the code does, see if it's actually happened before." It runs all these hypotheses and heuristics to understand: does it make sense? Is it meaningful? And then determine what to do with it.

距离"AI 运维分布式集群"还有多远？

Martin: How far away do you think we are — let's go back to query optimization — from having an AI do the job that a human used to do when it comes to query optimization?

Jad: I think very close.

Martin: Really? Running a distributed cluster — you've got James Cowing, PhD from MIT, who runs a distributed cluster, and if the cluster's down, the company doesn't work. Are we at the point where an AI can do that?

Jad: No, not yet. But look — when we started doing AI for coding, it was autocomplete. Nobody really knew to what extent you could build complex software using AI. When we were looking at it, we were like, "AI is never going to be able to build X or Y or Z." Then it basically broke through the expectations because we were able to model more and more complexity.

Martin: I'm a very simple thinker on this stuff. To me these models are distribution in, distribution out. It turns out you can train on all the code ever created and that manifold is pretty manageable. I don't know if operations is constrained in the same way. It feels to me more like the universe — heavy-tailed, exception-based, power laws, all the tough stuff for these models to learn. But I don't know — you're the one in the field.

Jad: I'll tell you — the history of systems, as you know, is: you always want to build a smart algorithm that does the efficient thing. The smart virtual memory management, the smart congestion control, the smart routing. And what do we do instead? Every single time —

Martin: We overprovision.

Jad: Every time.

Martin: Remember swap memory, where you'd swap to disk? Dude, if you did that, you were done. Your computer was dead. We literally overprovision RAM. And routing — how many adaptive routing algorithms are there? We'll respond to traffic, but you have oscillations. Screw it — we overprovision.

The history of systems is you don't predict stuff — you overprovision, because you can't. So in the operations side, either we build systems upfront that are overprovisioned so you don't have to do complex operational stuff, or maybe AI can do the way that a human being does — but I think it's very different than code, because you're dealing with exceptions, there's not a lot of data. But I don't know. I'm a VC.

Jad: The reason I'm more optimistic here is because I live in the world where what we do is actually deal with the observable world.

Martin: You're the literal expert on this — it's silly for me to even ask you.

Jad: Not at all. In my world, my assumption is that we have all the data — we know exactly when a new thing happens, when an exception emerges, when a workload changes. In my world, all of that has already been collected and streamed through.

Martin: But a model that is not trained on a grounded source for that stuff — that would be really hard, right?

Jad: But the story here isn't "Hey, Mr. Claude, here's a bunch of logs, is something going on?" It has to be much more able to run experiments and dive in — see what are the different shapes of possible causal chains that actually fit in the environment that exists.

Martin: I see — now I see what you're saying. The universe is heavy-tailed; the number of bad things that can happen is probably an exception thing — but the set of steps used to debug it is a manageable thing. That's what you can teach one of these models. And therefore, if you give it the right signals, it can go through a number of steps to actually constrain this problem.

Jad: Exactly.

Martin: Interesting.

Jad: So it really is taking the role of the human. Remember the whole chaos engineering wave?

Martin: And the reason it didn't go anywhere is: you're very quickly trying to reduce a state space that was atoms-in-the-universe-sized, and actually make that manageable. It was the human being that would go through steps that would do that debugging. This is what you're saying the AI would do.

Jad: Yes. The goal isn't to have the model just say "this is what happens." It's: "Run through this workflow to determine what happened." We're trying that also on the security side — "Hey, something behavioral is different in your environment, the cardinalities of various entities, that becomes a perturbation in the universe." We feed that into an AI: "Come up with a bunch of possible causal chains that exist, then verify if any of those fit the pattern of the data we actually see."

Martin: That seems even harder — because the operations one, the argument is the system can get into very rare broken states and there are a lot of those. The security one seems even harder, because this isn't just the natural order of rare states — you actually have an adversary that is intentionally trying to find rare states.

So it may be that code becomes solved, operations takes a little longer, and security takes a lot longer.

MP3 的故事：无穷集合的直觉陷阱

Jad: Also — think about it, the whole world is sort of quantized to a certain extent. The Planck length — is that what physicists say?

Martin: I don't know, I'm not a physicist. Constant.

Jad: I literally don't know what I'm talking about right now, but I actually think spacetime is discretized into a Planck length. But yes — I agree with what you just said. For operations and systems in general, there is a discretization of the possible states and the paths through them.

Martin: There might be a ton of them.

Jad: There might be a ton of them.

Martin: I'm going to tell you — remember Sundar, who was in our grad school group? Yeah. In their ear. Yeah. I remember he came to me once and he was looking very sad. "Martin, I just had this really sad realization — if you take any MP3 (remember MP3s, the music for us), MP3s have a finite length, let's say four minutes, four megabytes. That means there's a finite number of songs in the universe."

Because it's all made of bits, right? Four megabytes — you could just enumerate every one of those concepts. "I'm so sad in this notion of the finiteness of music." Literally we were walking on the Dish when he had this conversation. And I'm like, "Motherfucker, dude — do you know how quickly you've overcome the atoms in the universe? You haven't even gotten to a kilobyte, right? It's like two to the two to the two." What are you talking about? Be happy.

Jad: Two to the two to the two — four megabytes.

Martin: Four megabytes. You like — this is so much state. Be happy. That's effectively infinite.

So I do think at some level we underestimate the number of states that systems can get into. From the perspective of a VC that looks at these companies — the ones trying to tackle operations are having a tough go of it. It seems much tougher than those tackling code. I think it's a much tougher problem.

Jad: 100%, I agree. It is a much tougher problem — and not just because the systems themselves have external random loads, or somebody shipped a new thing into production without telling anybody, or there's some state that happens when this and this and this happen and then you end up in a deadlock. It's also because it involves humans a lot more, and not just one human who's the coder.

Martin: The pools of knowledge are distributed too.

Jad: Exactly. And the interactions between what it takes to connect the pieces and put them together.

But ultimately — when I think about where AI is and what the possible futures are — code to me is a microcosm. Maybe I'm too fatalistic, maybe too pessimistic about how the world works, and I think of everything as following some probabilistic path. If we can make it work in code, we can continue expanding that level of complexity bit by bit, adding layers until we can handle those problems.

Martin: It's not fatalistic — it's the opposite. That's very optimistic. For me, I don't think the universe gives up its secrets that easily. But we'll see. This is kind of the big question, and as yet it's not an answered question.

AI 的"宇宙问题"：代码世界 vs 真实世界

Jad: A lot of things that, as humans, we think of as being random or impossible to tackle — that's what we saw with coding. Initially people thought the possible world of all these things that you can implement in code are kind of limited, and you can't really get a system to potentially understand the full complexity of a human brain required. But I think over time it'll all —

Martin: It's so funny that I'm actually telling you this and you're the VC looking into the future. Well, I'll tell you my view. The study of these models is: you train on data, and that represents a distribution. That distribution is useful or not. When you train on language, the fact that it's useful says that humans are so remarkable because they've looked at the universe — which is this very high-dimensional system — and they've reduced it to a manifold that's actually useful for a model.

But that's different than the universe. There's a reduction from this high dimensionality to language — language is much less dimensional. Code is a reduction of all the operational states of a machine into the instructions that make it run. There's still a disconnect between the instructions / description and the actual running of the universe, the actual running of the system.

I think we can make gains toward it. But you're kind of converging on simulation. There are things that are computationally irreducible — you have to run it to get the answer. You can't just predict it. So maybe we're at an event horizon where models will solve anything you don't have to actually simulate to get the answer from.

Jad: But why do you have to think about it in terms of "it'll have to answer the question now," as opposed to being able to simulate — being able to plan its own execution to gain the information it needs?

Martin: Maybe that's where we're going. Fair enough.

Jad: There's a lower-dimensional space — the steps you would take — that we can reduce a whole bunch with AI. And then whatever steps that need something that it can't do, it can create the code to do, or simulate.

The point you're making though: the model can't actually go and figure out the additional dimensions of the world that we need to find, to model the universe into its world. That's probably true. But can it actually simulate a scientist sufficiently to get to that point? Maybe.

反问：VC 工作里有多少能被 AI 驱动？

Jad: Can I ask you a question? How much of the VC work do you think is something that an AI can drive?

Martin: My model for VC is that it's very relationship-driven. I have a belief that markets are actually pretty efficient — it's not about finding the company nobody else finds. People all find the right company. I also have the model that tech is net positive, and I'm optimistic about all tech. I don't worry about TAM.

So the key is access: raising money is access, ability to win deals, ability to add value after that happens. A lot of that is stuff startups just can't naturally do — recruit big execs, help with that. The way I think about venture, you kind of have to be a human being to do it, because that's the actual job. If you gave an AI a simulated universe where it could reward-hack building trust relationships — fine — but that would have to be —

That said, I have seen analysis done by AI that is as good or better than any junior analyst I've ever worked with. For the analysis piece, they're great. But I think this is more an indictment on VCs' ability to analyze than it is how powerful the models are. It's all a kabuki show and bullshit. The right VCs — tech is net positive, tech waves always add value, let's find the best company and invest in it, markets are efficient. The answer to this question is almost a technicality.

开放前沿：数字世界与真实世界的分野

Martin: One of the things I came here wanting to ask you: we started talking specifically about ops. But to me there's this world of AI writing code, which is kind of this abstract simulation world it lives in — and then there's the rest of the world.

Jad: The entire discussion is this. There's the digital world the AI lives in — the training data, the in-distribution world — and there's the actual world. Those are not necessarily the same. Quite often they're not. The question is: to what extent do you need to train an AI to be able to survive in a world?

I'm curious about the open spaces. We talked a little about operations. You said, "I don't know if it's going to be solved." I'm like, "Yeah, Martin, it's going to be solved." In my mind there are so many other things — for example, self-driving cars. For a long time we thought that's not going to happen, but it's clear it's actually going to be done. It's just taking time. What are the other next areas you think are lined up right after code?

Martin: My sense is: AI is going to continue to take off like wildfire for constrained domains — where the distribution of the solution space is the same as the distribution of the training set. The distribution of the syntax for code is the same as the training set. The distribution of generated images is the same as the training set.

In those areas it's going to continue to take off like wildfire. The domains where the distribution of the solution is the natural world — I think it's going to be much harder, take longer, and the economic equivalency is going to be much more difficult.

Self-driving is a great example. I remember when Sebastian Thrun won the DARPA Grand Challenge when I was at Stanford. We were like, "Hooray — self-driving cars are around the corner." It took 20 years and $170 billion of investment to get to worse unit economics than Uber.

Solving real problems where you have to deal with the distribution of the real universe is just much, much harder. I view AI as this general tool — a very effective tool. You have a distribution of data, and hopefully you can apply that to some problem. We're going to apply it to a bunch of stuff, and I think economic equilibrium is going to determine what works and what doesn't. It's a very general tool — a universal function approximator.

环境适配定律：改变世界以适配 AI

Jad: One of the things I said earlier — how AI was training humans to use it. I very often think about: some of the problems that seem intractable are because the world is kind of that way, and we're trying to fit AI or the tools we're building to manage the world as it is. But in some situations we actually tend to change the world to fit what we can actually do.

Martin: 100%. Of course. This is the story of robotics.

Jad: The automated data warehouse. The question that always came to my mind when we were looking at these data warehouses — the only one that worked was the one where it was like, "You know what — just automate the whole thing."

I wonder, as we expand the domain of what we want to solve with AI tools, to what extent we actually start modeling the world or changing the world and the things that can actually happen to fit what AI needs it to look like.

Martin: Right now a lot of AI operates in the digital world — and for that, literally the solution set is the same distribution as the training set. That's fine. When you're dealing with the real world, you can solve any problem you want — it's just a matter of compute and money, and the equilibrium point is going to be an economic one. One way you can impact that function you're doing equilibrium over is to constrain the environment, constrain the system.

We're now in this meta-economic-equilibrium flywheel where we're optimizing this super-general but very inefficient process with a solution set that people value. Listen — we've got 30 years of this and a lot of value is going to be created.

收尾：客户要省钱，不要 AI

Martin: You want to hear a funny story?

Jad: Yeah.

Martin: We built this AI thing — we're reaching out to customers. "Hey, we built this AI thing, we're helping customers become more reliable, here's what we're doing." They're like, "Great, we want to talk to you." We go on the call: "Hey, here's what we do, we built this system, helps you optimize your data, helps you reduce costs, and then helps you become more reliable because we can find these problems and solve them before they hit incidents."

They're like, "Wait, wait, wait — roll back. You said you can save 90% of our Datadog bills? That's what I want to buy."

Jad: Yeah.

Martin: "But — but — the AI thing?" "No, no, no, no. That's what we want to buy right now."

For code, you know, people just get it. They're like, "Oh — it just works." On the ops side, or anything beyond that, it's much harder to understand the actual value, put a dollar value to it, and pay out the door.

Jad: 100%.

Martin: From a coding standpoint, literally it's engineering productivity, which is one of the highest line items. So it's just very straightforward.

Jad: Exactly. But you can also think about it — it's SRE productivity, or your business going down. Maybe you can save an incident and what the cost is. It's weird — how people think about it outside of…

Martin: I also just think code was so magical because it was so good, and nobody thought that could happen. The operations stuff now — it's still pretty early.

Jad: It's still pretty early.

Martin: Alright. Well — listen, it's great to chat. Thanks, Jad.

Jad: Thanks.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：这不是一场关于"AI能力"的对话，而是一场关于"维度坍缩"的对话
整段访谈真正讨论的，其实是一个被双方都没点破的分水岭——**代码世界的本质是"降维后的宇宙"**。Martin 几乎说出了关键一句：人类之所以能把语言、代码训练进模型并有用，是因为"人类把高维宇宙压缩成了一个可用的流形(manifold)"。
换句话说，AI 之所以能写代码，不是因为它懂代码，而是因为**代码是人类替宇宙做好的"低维投影"**。所有编程语言都是人类数百年苦心积累的"宇宙压缩算法"。 而运维（operations）正相反——它是把那层压缩**解开**的过程，让程序重新落回高维、重尾、异常主导的真实物理世界里（内存、网络、电子迁移、运营商抽风、昨天在饮水机旁听来的那条部署变更）。
所以这场对话真正的隐喻是：**AI 学会了弹奏乐谱，但还没有学会在一场有空调嗡嗡声、观众咳嗽、麦克风反馈的音乐厅里即兴演出。** 这正是为什么 Jad 的公司 Greer 关键价值并不是模型，而是**那层把真实世界转成"AI 可以理解的低维信号"的采集管道**——护城河不在 AI 层，在传感层。
#

item.title: [Lex Clips] The famous braised pig's feet dish in Taiwan | Lex Fridman and Jensen Huang
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽略的隐喻：从"猪脚"到"芯片"的"整只动物"哲学

最让人意外的是 Jensen 那句"it's a whole food"。表面只是在为猪脚辩护——这是一道会把脚趾完整端上桌的菜，不像美式料理把一切处理成"去识别化"的肉块。但如果你知道 Nvidia 的护城河恰恰是"全栈"（whole stack）——从硅、驱动、CUDA、cuDNN、到数据中心、再到机器人栈的垂直整合——那这个"whole"就不只是一个饮食偏好，而是一种被身体记忆的工程直觉：他不害怕看见脚趾，就像他不害怕让 Nvidia 下沉到硬件、也上浮到软件。美国人吃肉只吃"中间那段"，恰如硅谷大多数公司只做"中间那层"。台湾卤味的"nose-to-tail"精神，和 Nvidia 的"edge-to-cloud"精神，是同一种人格在两个尺度上的显影。

一个真正的跨域连接："Novideo"问题 ≈ 风味的后天习得曲线

Jensen 看着镜头说"Most people call it Novideo"的瞬间，紧接着就有人把猪脚递过来——这个剪辑顺序其实比他们意识到的要讽刺得多。品牌名的拼写障碍，和"acquired taste"是同一条曲线：陌生 → 排斥 → 重复暴露 → 突然成为口腔/口语的默认设置。心理学上这叫"mere exposure effect"。所以 Nvidia 过去三十年其实不是在"做显卡"，而是在反复给世界喂同一道猪脚：第一次你皱眉说"这是什么"，第十次你开始发对音，第一百次你忘了它曾经陌生过。GPU 加速计算这件事能从游戏卡变成 AI 基础设施，走的是和卤猪脚打进美国餐桌一样的渗透路径——不靠教育，靠让你没得选的日常化。

一个几乎没人注意的细节：权力的"低姿态"展示

一位市值数万亿的 CEO，身边坐着他的父母，让 Lex 当临时摄影师，被母亲纠正吃相，还要被打趣"My parents won't judge me cuz I'm the cameraman"。这段看似闲笔，其实是一种反向的权力展示——真正坐稳位置的人，不需要在镜头前表演稳。更妙的是中间冒出的一句"Teamwork"，发生在两人配合夹起一块猪脚的瞬间。这是整段里信息密度最高的一个词：Jensen 的管理哲学从来不是"扁平组织"或"直接汇报 60 个人"的那套工程术语，而是一种餐桌式的协同——你夹一下、我接一下、不要让它掉。他不是在采访里讲团队，他是在吃团队。硅谷过去二十年的管理书写了那么多页，可能都比不上这一帧——两双筷子、一只脚趾、三个字。

📝 转录文本

开场：父母同行

You don't mind my parents coming, right? — No. — They just love this place so much.

这道菜是什么

So we're having some braised pig's feet. Have you ever had pig's feet before? I'm guessing it's a bit of an acquired taste.

— Actually, it tastes good. Okay. Look. Pay attention to— Hey, it's a whole food. Get ready to—

— So good.

So this is pork, this is tofu, egg, and that's the pig's feet.

— Wow.

It sounds iffy, but it tastes really good.

— It is so good.

镜头后的插科打诨

My parents won't judge me cuz I'm the cameraman. He knows how to multitask. Almost messed it. Okay. Got it. Teamwork. She's going in. That's the toe right there.

关于品牌名："Novideo"

I think it's a branding issue. It's all about the name. It probably took years for people to learn how to spell Nvidia correctly.

— Most people call it Novideo.

— Novideo.

— Yeah.

Look at that toe. Look at that toe. That's a good toe.

美国的台湾菜

Does America do Taiwanese food good or not?

— No. But it's starting to do better.

插曲：路人与寒暄

What's that girl wearing? Everything.

— Rex. Good to meet you. Great getting a chance to chat.

— I have a brother. I told everybody that Jensen—

— Yeah. Yeah, Jensen and I are just chatting how when he is learning about new things, maybe learning about new companies, he uses Perplexity AI computer.

— Yeah. Dude, he uses Perplexity computer.

— Okay. Awesome. Beatles in the 60s.

Jensen 看着镜头说"Most people call it Novideo"的瞬间，紧接着就有人把猪脚递过来——这个剪辑顺序其实比他们意识到的要讽刺得多。品牌名的拼

item.title: [Business of Sport] Football Regulator’s Warning Shot, Pantomime Premier League, Fury vs AJ & F1 Lands in Africa
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"潘托剧化"的英超：悬念消失后，剩下的是加了星号的胜利

曼城案真正恐怖的地方，不是判决本身，而是它把英超变成了一个量子叠加态的联赛——每场比赛的结果都同时"算数"和"不算数"，必须等到仲裁庭敲下法槌才能坍缩。Charles 对自己的情绪困惑其实指向一个更深的产品学问题：切尔西球迷现在应该希望曼城赢，因为曼城赢球等于偷其他对手的分，而这些分最后会被没收返还。竞争的方向感被反转了。

这就是为什么安菲尔德没有预期的敌意，只有冷漠。愤怒需要确定的敌人，冷漠才是叙事崩塌的信号。而真正的跨领域类比在这里：曼城现在的处境，等同于一支面临退市威胁的股票——每一次股价波动都带着"可能全部作废"的折价。Sky Sports 下一轮续约卡在这个"折价期"开场的头两场，是教科书级别的 overhang 时机灾难。意甲衰落的加速器"电话门"不是单一事件，而是产品可信度一旦被打上问号，国际转播费的下行是复利式的——这是英超目前真正在面对的风险。

二、董事会的秘密：英超俱乐部其实是硅谷早期创业公司

报告里最震撼的那个数字——66% 的俱乐部若老板停输血，撑不过 90 天——听起来像足球危机，其实是一个标准的 Startup Runway 问题。财务总监每月末前十天给老板发消息"请打款，否则这周发不出工资"——这几乎是 YC 孵化器里 pre-seed 公司最常见的内部沟通。英超百亿产业的底层运行机制，和一个月烧 50 万美元的 B 轮创业公司惊人地同构。

这就引出了一个 Kogan 自己可能没点破的角度：他引入的"压力测试""业务计划"要求，不是从体育监管来的，而是直接从 2008 年金融危机后的巴塞尔协议 III 平移过来的——他把俱乐部当银行管了。注意他的措辞："资本要求""兜底资金""清算路径"——每一个词都是 FSA/PRA 对银行用的术语。英格兰足球正在被银行化，而没人意识到这意味着什么：下一个十年，俱乐部 CFO 的招聘标准会从"懂体育"变成"懂监管合规"。足球行业的组织基因正在被静悄悄地替换。

另一个被忽略的隐藏信号：六/八号防守中场成为最贵资产类别，均价欧元 1000 万。表面是战术趋势，底层是劳动力市场定价的变相证实——现代英超的核心能力是打断对方节奏的能力，而不是制造节奏的能力。这反向说明英超联赛的强度已经让"仅仅是优秀的足球运动员"不够用了，必须是运动员+足球员。Wirtz 在周末被身体碾压的画面，就是这个市场结论的终端呈现。

三、F1 的美国危机：真正杀死收视率的不是比赛，是免费试用期

68% 的迈阿密收视暴跌，所有媒体把它归咎于"赛事不精彩""Verstappen 碾压"。都错了。看前三场澳日中——跌幅是 4%、1%、0%。再看第四场迈阿密——瞬间 68%。这是一条典型的订阅服务流失曲线：Apple TV+ 的免费试用通常 7 天—3 个月，前三场正好覆盖试用期尾声。观众不是不爱 F1，是不愿意为 F1 单独付钱。

这是跨平台迁移的隐性税，WWE 从 USA Network 迁移到 Peacock 时经历过几乎一模一样的曲线。F1 从 ESPN 的捆绑有线信号迁移到 Apple TV+ 的独立订阅，等于把"沙发上随手切过去看一眼"的被动观众全部剔除——而这些被动观众恰恰是过去三年 Drive to Survive 转化来的新粉，他们的粘性最弱。你花了五年把他们吸引进来，一个合同把他们重新筛了一遍。

更深的讽刺：F1 现在同时患了叙事缺失症（规则改革杀死了竞争张力）和分销摩擦症（订阅模式筛掉了被动观众），而拳击患的是反向的病——分销太宽松（任何电视都能看），叙事太混乱（WBA、WBC、IBF、WBO 四条平行"世界冠军"线，没人知道冠军是谁）。而 One Championship 的崛起路径，和 2000 年代初 PDC 对 BDO 的分化惊人地同构——真正的颠覆不是改变战斗方式，而是垄断排名系统。谁拥有"冠军"这个标签的所有权，谁就拥有这个运动。

四、一个被所有人忽略的意外联系

Zak Brown 一年拿 1 亿美元（基本工资 1000 万 + 增值股权激励 9000 万），这不是体育经理薪酬，这是硅谷 CEO 的激励结构。McLaren 估值从 7.4 亿涨到 50 亿，Brown 拿走增值的 ~2%——这完全符合晚期 PE 的 Carry 结构。F1 车队的治理模式正在从家族—俱乐部结构转向风投—科技公司结构。而当你把这件事和前面的"足球俱乐部银行化"放在一起看，一个更大的图景浮现：整个体育产业正在被金融业和科技业的组织范式殖民。Rwanda 花 1% 的 GDP 建 F1 赛道，和一个主权基金做 VC 投资没有本质差别——他们买的不是赛道，是国家品牌的流动性。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open — Teasers

The current walking assumption of everybody in football in England is that, well, the Premier League will carry on being really successful. But this is serious. This is really serious. This could start to cause problems in terms of the general international perspective of the Premier League itself.

17 clubs across the EFL and National League will lose money even if their players played for free. What's happening is about 10 days before the end of each month, the finance director is sending a message to the owner saying, "Please, can you wire across X amount or the club will go bust?"

It's a little bit sad this is happening when Joshua's 36 and Fury is 38. But does that mean it's gonna be a crap fight? No. To me, this is a problem that boxing has and I find it really hard to properly put a lot of my eggs in the basket of a sport where there's a very real chance that I can't see the best fighters against the best fighters when I want them to be fighting.

Formula One made a big announcement that Grand Prix's were returning to Africa. Rwanda is going to host the first Grand Prix since 1993. A lot of the growth and the reason why a lot of the big tech companies are getting involved is on the premise that F1's finally cracked America. Miami had a 68% viewership decline. If the TV ratings aren't there, you haven't really cracked America.

Opening Banter

Good afternoon, Charlie. How are you? Hi, Charlie. You look a little bit sheepish. Do I? No, no, you do. I think you look sheepish. I think you look sheepish because I think you've just received a bollocking from one of your own engineers here saying that you need to speak up more. No, was it show a bit more energy? Oh, no, it's actually worse, wasn't it? Come on, show a bit more energy. I don't think anyone's ever accused you of not having energy. I know. It's the reverse, Kirsty, as you just described it. Yeah, exactly, when you start getting bollockings from your junior staff. [LAUGHTER] I don't know what I've done to upset him. It's a great reflection on the internal culture here that they feel empowered to make these criticisms. Yeah, look, that's how we run the ship.

Manchester City Return: A "Hollow Despair" Weekend

Anyway, what an interesting weekend of football we've just had. Well, I guess, sorry, again, coming out on Friday, the weekend seems a little bit further away. We're recording this on Wednesday. It's still relatively fresh in the mind. After all the chaos that has ensued in the international break of Man City being found guilty of all their charges, this was the first time we saw them back on the pitch. And I just felt a level of hollow despair, depression, flatness around this, I think, as a fan. I think that's because you saw, oh no, this is what the next few months are going to look like. It's not even just today. This is going to be the same at least for the next few months and potentially even beyond that.

And this is where it does become a major problem for the Premier League, which is that, okay, just in the instance of the whole thing coming out, the verdict coming out, in a way adds to the drama of the Premier League and that would have been huge eyeballs on that game. I'd love to see when they eventually come out the ratings for that game — would have been absolutely massive. But as the weeks go on, it's no longer exciting anymore. It drops back into every round of matches comes with an asterisk saying, well, you know, but what we're seeing here, is that really going to be a mirage? Is that really the case? Are they really top of the table? Are teams that are currently six or seven points off them, six or seven points at the top? Or are they six or seven points off a team that's about to get a massive points deduction? So it's a real problem.

The Appeal Timeline

What has become clear is that the plan is that appeal is going to be heard quickly. That's become very clear. And I think that's absolutely necessary. Have you seen something that says that? Because I was listening to David Kogan in his interview and he said he thought it would be finished by the end of the season, to which point I really choked on my... No, he said this morning on the radio it would be done pretty much by Christmas. Oh, brilliant, because the BBC interview he did was by the end of the season.

I mean, the problem is that even that isn't necessarily the end of it because all the mood music coming out of City is that they're going to, quote, pursue all avenues, which presumably means judicial proceedings, right? So going outside of the football framework into the courts, the High Court, Supreme Court, and of course those types of things can take a very, very long time. But I'm not sure that those types of appeals forestall the actual punishment. I think the punishment would be levied and then the appeals to the High Court and the Supreme Court potentially are effectively legal action against the punishment and the verdict that have been levied.

So what we're actually looking at here, and perhaps this is what Kogan was referring to, is that we've got, first of all, an appeal process and then a sanction process. Those two things combined could take until February, March, which would just cast a very long shadow over everything else that's happening with the season.

The Confusion of Supporting Your Rival's Rival

It was strange though, wasn't it? In a game that normally you'd look forward to as one of the top games of the season, one of my favourite hobbies is watching Liverpool concede goals. And I was just sitting there as each one went in. And by the way, each one being exceptional. Yeah, great goals. I mean, the goals, Haaland's goal, Doku's goal and Cherki's goal were brilliant. And to not just be able to celebrate, appreciate that talent on the pitch was part of that feeling of just kind of maybe confusion as well. There was a confusion in my own emotions of having 30 whatever years of feeling a certain way about it and then suddenly questioning whether I could or should.

But I also sat there. It was interesting. I'd like to know your thoughts on it because what it's kind of done is it's manufactured. If you really look at what those games mean now, me as a Chelsea fan, I kind of should want City to win these games. Yeah. Because they're most likely going to lose these points. They're taking points off your rivals. And they're taking points off the rivals. So in the quest for whatever, top four or league titles or anything in and around that, if City win the games, it's helping any team that is chasing those other teams.

So they've kind of, in this whole situation, engineered a situation where the worst thing for me isn't watching City win matches, which feels weird in itself. But it just... it just felt like such a strange thing that was going on and that was just so un-Premier League. And if you listen to Gary Neville around it, you know, I mean, he was going, I don't want to do any City games. But it just felt like this very confusing...

Well, you're finding it hard to articulate. And I agree with you, it is hard to articulate. All I do know for sure, you know, speaking from the position of a sports promoter, is that this isn't good. When you've got people feeling confusion about what they're watching, and this won't just relate to City games, this will relate to all games at the top of the table, which is, what does this really mean, where do things sit, and all this type of stuff. It's just really bad for the product. It's really, really bad for the product.

The Calciopoli Parallel

And I am concerned, we'll come on to a moment about the overall state of football from a financial and business perspective. The current walking assumption of everybody in football in this country, in England, is that, well, the Premier League will carry on being really successful. And then it's a question of, well, how much money should come from the Premier League to the other clubs? And how can we get better cost controls and all that type of stuff? But this is big. This is serious. This is really serious. This could start to cause problems in terms of the general international perspective of the Premier League itself.

We should never forget that the catalyst for the downfall of Serie A — not the catalyst, but a major factor in the downfall of Serie A — was the Calciopoli scandal. A lot of people were interested in about that. And I think, you know, there were other factors as well. Serie A was probably already on the way down. But at the time of Calciopoli, it was only three years previously that they'd been the biggest spending league in the entire world. So it was quite recent. They weren't far off the Premier League at that point. And since then, coincidence or not, there's been a massive and precipitate decline.

So, leave aside Premier League itself, English football as an ecosystem cannot afford for the Premier League to be a suboptimal product. Everything relates on the revenues that the Premier League spits out.

Impact on Sky Sports & TV Rights

And that's an interesting point. Do you think this presents a problem for things like the Sky Sports contract, who buy the most prestigious league in the world and pay billions to broadcast it, and essentially now, for however many months this go on for, are broadcasting something or verging on a pantomime?

Well, that will depend on what it does for TV ratings. Right? So if we start to see a drop off in TV ratings, then obviously the renegotiation, the domestic deal is quite imminent next year. Yeah, I think it's next year. So it's really bad timing as well. If you're at the start of a five year cycle, then you say, OK, well, let's ride through this one and we'll pick up over time. But if we — because it's come quite early in this season, particularly given the international break, there's been very few matches in total. So we've still got the vast majority of the Premier League season ahead. And if it is the case that we don't get resolution in terms of what the sanctions might be, assuming that they don't win their appeal, until March, that's just a massive chunk of the season where people gonna be going, well, you know, I'm not really sure. It's all gonna be decided in the courtroom ultimately. Think about any sporting competition when you know in advance it's gonna be decided in the courtroom. Doesn't it remove a little bit the interest to actually watch it fully?

So with the domestic deal up for a negotiation, I think maybe, maybe it's international this year, next year and domestic the year after actually. Anyway, either way, the next cycle... The TV deals are up in the next 18 months, right? That's when they're going to be renegotiated. So it's terrible timing if they do see a dip in ratings.

Well, I think you're right when you said, look, you would have seen a big spike at the weekend. Everyone was tuning in. I actually — say disappointed — I thought the atmosphere was far less hostile than I anticipated. But I expected Anfield to be absolutely spitting, considering as well the associations they have with this cheating scandal and the trophies that they could consider they've lost out on. But if there is a level of apathy to it, which, you know, apathy is the worst thing of all in professional sports.

Well, it is. And I've had a level, I don't know, I mean, again, you're not a fan. I've had a level of apathy towards Man City for years. I've never really minded about them as a — I've always wanted the Arsenals to lose or the Liverpools to lose, but because I never really had a deep association with City fans or, you know, a long history of hating another team, they never really bothered me that much. The apathy that I had towards City then kind of moved at the weekend towards the game in general and the sport. And that, as I said to round it off, I think that is the big challenge that they have to overcome.

And if people do drop off and stop watching it, then it wouldn't surprise me at all if Sky Sports turn around and started causing problems for that deal, which they would be in their right to do. And which, by the way, is not implausible anyway. It's perfectly plausible that Sky Sports in the next deal — don't forget in the last deal the Premier League had to chuck in extra matches to try to keep the levels at pretty much the same. And so if you see a drop off, and particularly given that Sky Sports has made significant losses in various years recently, it wouldn't take very much for Sky Sports to say, look, guys, you know, we can't afford to pay you what we have been paying you before. And then everything else that we've been talking about in terms of what we're about to talk about in terms of the financial health of the English game really starts to be called into question. Because even relatively small reductions in revenue, as we will see in a moment when we discuss the State of the Game report, can cause much bigger problems.

Look, the bottom line is, I agree with you. It was a really odd occasion. I think probably most football fans wanted it to be a really good match that Liverpool won. And then everyone gets fired up and says, OK, Liverpool are back. It's, you know, it's the Southern City. It was deeply unsatisfactory for City to win 3-0 after Liverpool having a player arguably a bit unfortunately sent off. It just sort of led the entire thing to a bit of an anti-climax when, as you said, the atmosphere hadn't been at its absolute fever pitch that we might have expected to either way. I think if Klopp had been there, it probably would have been. Yeah, maybe. Yeah, probably, that's right. A disappointing weekend all round, and I think we should all be just checking and tracking our emotions as the next few weeks go by.

The Promoted Clubs Making Waves

Well, Charlie, what it did also bring up was before we move on, another look at the strength of the teams that have come up and the successes that they are having in the early parts of this season. Which again was underlined last night when Coventry thumped Newcastle. Was it last night or the night before? Two nights ago. So you had Coventry beat Newcastle. Yeah. A Hull draw with Everton. Yeah. And you had Ipswich beat Fulham. You're turning it around in the last few minutes.

But the reason I mention it is because our friends at Transfer Room have just released a very interesting report on the 2026 summer transfer window. And a big part of that was actually looking at the spend of those clubs coming up. And we did talk about it at the beginning of the season. Those three teams that got promoted spent €559 million. The Saudi Pro League in total spent €476 million, to put that into context. But it all seems to be working for them.

Well, having just discussed something that's quite clearly very bad for the Premier League product, for the three promoted teams to be competitive is obviously very good for the Premier League product, right? It means that even the shoulder games, the types of games which maybe the broadcasters wouldn't rate so much, but they show them because you have to show a certain number of games for each club, etc. If Coventry come out and play like that against Newcastle, then the broadcasters go, wow, this league's getting even deeper. It's getting even more competitive. It's getting even more exciting. We really don't know in any game who's going to come out on top, if those teams are going to be competitive as well.

So, look, it's early days and there's a long history of newly promoted clubs doing relatively well in the first part of the season only to find that the winter wears them down and they get stuck in a bit of a rut and the Premier League just eventually sort of eats away at their sort of optimism in their early seasons. But I think, you know, in the case of Coventry, they had a poor start, but as the team has gelled, they pulled it around. Ipswich have been, I think, sort of more or less competitive from the start, give or take. They were a bit unfortunate in one or two early games.

The Hull Phenomenon

And Hull have been the big surprise package. I think, I mean, Hull is sort of, you know, pretty much a walking assumption by most people, including the bookmakers, that Hull would go straight back down. Because they were very, in performance terms, very fortunate to come up. You know, they came up through the playoffs, who are probably the best team in the playoffs, had been removed from the playoffs. Hull themselves had finished quite a long way behind the automatic promotion places. Their underlying performance numbers on XG were terrible. You know, how they even got into playoffs is difficult to say. Then they conceded like the fourth most goals, I think, or something, wasn't it? And, I mean, their XG numbers were like sort of bottom six, right?

So for them to have, you know, managed to produce a competitive Premier League squad when they were probably more or less a mid-table championship squad last season — I think is quite remarkable and probably needs a bit of looking at in terms of the recruitment that they have done because that is difficult, right? That is really, really difficult to turn that kind of level around in the space of three months. Particularly when you're in the playoffs because you don't know you're going to be in the Premier League until the start of June, right? So all those conversations that you want to have with players that you want to bring in, the other teams already in the Premier League can start having in January and February. Teams who have been automatically promoted can start having at the start of May. But you're not in a position to have that conversation. If you go to the agents of a player that you think you might want to sign if you make the Premier League in mid-May and you're only in the semi-finals of the playoffs, the agent will go, well, give us a shout in a few weeks' time because my player's not coming to the Championship.

So I think that job — and let's see if their performance level improves, you know, is, keeps going. But it would be a remarkable achievement, a really remarkable football department achievement if Hull were able to be, well, frankly, were not to get relegated. Yeah. That would be a remarkable achievement.

Pressure on the Established Mid-Table

Well, do you know what it also, you know, puts a boot up the back of a few of the more established Premier League [sides] because they've been — well, is this the discussion that we need to start having? Because if all of the promoted teams are competitive and you're talking about Bournemouth, Brighton and Brentford being at the moment sort of mid-table and up, in terms of Bournemouth at 18th right now as it happens — as it happens — but if you look at their performance levels, doesn't look too bad. But you're looking at some clubs and you're wondering, if you look at all the numbers around Newcastle and you're thinking, hmm, if all three of the promoted clubs are really competitive, are you 100% safe? Fulham are in trouble. We actually called that at the start of the season. Yeah. It's all pretty tight, isn't it? Man United. I mean... Spurs outplayed them. We can talk about that later on.

Transfer Room Report: £11 Billion & the Premier League's 37%

I want to come back on to the transfer room report. Because as you say, one thing it did highlight, which we've discussed before, is the massive spending by the newly promoted teams, which does look like it's been reasonably successful. But it really did spell out quite starkly stuff that we were discussing at the time, but didn't yet have the full numbers on. Which is that the total amount spent globally on this was £11 billion, of which the Premier League was almost 40%. Right. 37% of all spending was by Premier League clubs globally.

Now, just to put that in context, La Liga was 10%, Serie A 7%, Bundesliga 6%, Ligue 1 5%. Right. So if you add all those together, you're at 28% of total global spending compared to the Premier League clubs' 37%. Right? I mean, it is quite astonishing. And we'll come on to in the IFR's report a slightly concerning element of that. But it does demonstrate, I think, you know, the extent to which really now we're talking about that 11 billion number is reached mostly by an increasingly small number of very high tariff transfers, right?

So that 11 billion, yes, it's going up, but it's not going up because everyone's spending. It's going up because there are 5, 10, 15 very big transfers, right? Which make up a big chunk of that total number. And we can probably name them, right? Those big Premier League 100 million plus deals, right? The Barcleys, the Rogers, the... If you get 10 of those, then that is in itself 10% of all global spending just on those 10 players, right? And that includes all of the spending all over the world, even at much lower levels and all this type of stuff. So it is quite astonishing.

Who Are the Net Sellers?

I thought it was also quite interesting in the report to see what the biggest selling leagues were. So where are the players coming from? Premier League were the biggest selling league as well, weren't they? Yes. But mostly to itself. Yes. So this was like net selling. These are the ones who were the biggest net sellers, right? So you've got the old stalwarts of Belgium and Portugal. You know, being really high caliber leagues, really high quality football leagues, where there are a lot of clubs that aren't that rich and who basically sell their players every summer. France, of course, is now becoming more like that type of league because outside of PSG, now they don't have a TV deal, their revenues increasingly are much more similar to a Portugal league in terms of total league revenues.

But even PSG were about £170 million in the green, weren't they? Yeah. On the transfer. Yeah. I mean, they conducted, I remember, they conducted, I think, you know, they replaced their front line with three £50-ish million players. They sold Barcley for £123 million and they sold... That looks like cracking business, doesn't it? It's early days, but he looked like a fish out of water on the weekend against City, I thought, as it verts. Yeah. Yes. And has done now for... I mean, I think he's played 65-ish games now. So his body of work is significant.

The New Premier League Archetype: Athlete First, Footballer Second

I thought that game was interesting in terms of delineating what type of footballer really is effective at Premier League level. Because until he got sent off, Ryan Gravenberch was Liverpool's best player. Big, striding, powerful player who can go past people, who can physically force his way around the field. And what it's looking like increasingly — I know a lot of people are very, well, there are quite a few football traditionists who are very critical about this — is it's increasingly quite difficult in the Premier League these days to be just a good footballer. You've got to be a good athlete. And that, it just really, really looked that way on, you know, when I was watching Barcley and Wirtz and just thinking, do you have the physical abilities to be able to do what the Premier League needs you to do?

Well, it's interesting you say that. I mean, I'm — joking aside about Chelsea's performance, you could see the difference with Caicedo back in the team versus not being back in the team. I mean, the quality of the sitting midfielder. And it links into this excellent report. By the way, it's packed, this report. So I'm going to put it in the comments, guys, and you can have a look at it. But one of the other things in it was the defensive midfielder now being the most premium asset across the board. Yes, I saw that. That was really interesting.

So these days, increasingly, the six and six-eight players — so that's the defensive centre midfielder and maybe one who can do a bit of both — those are now becoming the most valuable players ahead of strikers. Yeah. And I think it was 10 million euros, they said, is the average. Now, as an average, that may seem low because you're picturing the 100 million. As an average across every defensive midfielder sold, that's a high average. That indicated the shift. And we've seen it for a long time, right? Because a lot of the signings over the last few years, particularly the highest ones, have actually been in and around that part of the pitch. But to actually see it on paper now hitting, I would say a consistent — and there's an overall trend as opposed to anecdotal evidence. Exactly. I thought that was very interesting.

Saudi Pro League Pullback

Interesting also to see the massive decrease in Saudi Pro League spending. Yeah. As I said, with the 476 million euros of which Al-Hilal was over half of it, I think. Yeah. So what do you think that means? Do you think — I mean, it's basically just becoming less of an option on a lucrative exit for clubs, isn't it?

Absolutely. There was a couple of years when Premier League clubs could clear the decks of the players that they didn't want and just know, okay, look, he's still got a good name.
