item.title: [Lex Clips] Jensen Huang gets mobbed by engineers in Taiwan | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、Jensen 现象：硅片第一次拥有了"人格引力场"

视频里最震撼的不是技术，而是一位芯片 CEO 被工程师围堵的场景。这在半导体史上几乎没有先例——Intel 的 Grove、Krzanich、Gelsinger 走在街上没人认识；台积电张忠谋在西方几乎无面孔。而现在一个做 GPU 的黄仁勋，被叫做"Beatles"。

这背后藏着一个被忽略的转折：AI 让硅第一次"可见"。 过去三十年，芯片是一个"消失的产业"——它越成功，越不可见（埋在服务器里、嵌在手机里）。而生成式 AI 让每一次对话都能被追溯到"是哪块芯片在算"，于是硬件突然有了叙事权。黄仁勋不是靠营销成为明星的，他是第一个"被 token 抬起来"的硬件家。

跨领域连接：这其实复刻了 19 世纪末爱迪生-特斯拉时代的工程师崇拜——那也是基础设施（电）从不可见转向可见的时刻。每当底层能源被重新定义，底层能源的"面孔"就会被神化。你现在看到的 Jensenity，是算力即电力这个事实的社会化外显。

二、"The more you buy, the more you make" 不是销售话术，是经济学范式切换

Jensen 一句玩笑："The more you buy, the more you make." 看似销售技巧，但真正该震惊的是他顺手完成了一次经济学模型的替换：

  • x86 时代：CPU 卖的是"核"，经济学单位是 dollars per core——这是租金经济（Rent Economy），客户买的是"位置"，像买地皮。
  • AI 时代：GPU 卖的是"token"，经济学单位是 tokens per second——这是生产经济（Production Economy），客户买的是"产出速率"，像买织布机。

这个转变比它听起来剧烈得多——它意味着数据中心第一次有了"产能利用率"这个工业指标。过去数据中心是房地产（出租），现在是工厂（生产）。这也解释了为什么 Jensen 疯狂压缩组装时间（2 小时 → 5 分钟）：在租金经济里，建造慢没关系；在生产经济里，每多一天没建完，就是少卖的 token。

出人意料的一点：这其实复现了第一次工业革命的核心转折——从"土地租金"到"工厂产出"的价值计量切换。换句话说，黄仁勋不是在卖芯片，他是在给整个数字文明重装一次 18 世纪。

三、两个被埋没的"反直觉金句"——以及它们之间的隐秘共振

视频里有两句话被当成闲聊带过，但其实是贯穿 NVIDIA 工程哲学的核心：

"Things that are easy to build are also reliable."
"Speed is not everything. Sometimes you have to pause and think."

表面上，一句讲硬件，一句讲对话；但它们是同一个原理的两种投射：降低认知负荷 = 提升系统稳健性。

  • 一个 GPU 板子，如果组装步骤从 2 小时压到 5 分钟，不是因为"工人更快"，而是因为结构本身消除了可能出错的决策点——这叫 affordance design，是 Don Norman 认知心理学中的概念被硬件化。
  • 一个人，如果边说边想，就等于让"输出"和"推理"共享同一条带宽——这也是认知负荷过载。所以 Jensen 承认自己"打字能思考，说话不能"。

跨领域的意外连接：这和 Toyota 生产系统的 jidoka（自働化）原则、以及海军核反应堆的 Rickover 工程哲学完全同构——"易建造 = 高可靠"是一条自然律，不是软要求。而当 Jensen 把这条原则同时应用在钢板和自己的大脑上时，你看到的其实是同一个人把工业工程原理应用到了元认知。

四、最隐藏的一个信号：Wabi-sabi 时刻

视频里最容易被跳过的是他盯着一块（可能是有瑕疵的）芯片或样品说：

"When I was young, I would think that's not good. But now, I love wabi-sabi."

一个把 "zero defect" 当成信仰的半导体帝国掌舵人，公开表达对不完美的审美偏好——这是一个哲学级别的信号。

我的大胆预测：这不是闲话，这暗示 NVIDIA 内部已经在接受一个未来的事实——在 Blackwell 之后的尺度上，"完美良率"将不再是经济最优解。当芯片大到晶圆尺寸（wafer-scale, 像 Cerebras），当 chiplet 组合复杂到一定程度，容错架构会压过完美良率。Jensen 的 wabi-sabi 不是审美，是在为"冗余容错式计算"做心理铺垫。

换句话说：当他开始爱不完美，就是他准备卖不完美的时候。

📝 转录文本

偶遇与寒暄

Lex Fridman: Hey Jensen. Jensen Huang: Thanks. How's it going? Lex: Good to see you. Jensen: Welcome to Taiwan. Hey guys, do you know who this is? Crowd: Yes. Jensen: The great — Crowd: Yes. Love you. Lex: I love you, too. [laughter] Jensen: He's known worldwide as Lex, just like me, Jensen. Lex: You know you made it when you're just one — Jensen: You're just one name. Lex: Beyoncé. Jensen: Beyoncé. Lex: It's incredible. So much kindness. You're a rockstar. Jensen: Hey guys. Nice to see you. Nice to see you guys. Nice to see you guys.

"Jensenity" — 工程师的簇拥

Lex: Okay, this is legit. This is pretty insane. Jensenity. Jensen: Mike, do you know the famous Lex Fridman? Mike: Good to meet you. Jensen: Look at this guy. He went — he's just traveling through Asia. [laughter] Does everybody know the famous Lex Fridman? Fan: Stop it. Jensen, I love you. Jensen: Look at this. Look at this. [laughter]

100% 液冷与装配时间的革命

Jensen: No cables. No hoses. 100% liquid cooled. Lex: Yes. Jensen: Last generation Grace Blackwell was only 80% liquid cooled. Now it's 100% liquid cooled. From 2 hours to assemble, it's now 5 minutes. Things that are easy to build are also reliable. Lex: Officially in full production, right? Jensen: Yeah, full production now. Lex: Incredible, right? Jensen: Yeah, it's incredible. Lex: All this. Jensen: Everything.

CPU 的新经济学：从"核"到"token"

Lex: And the very CPU, you're full in on the CPU. I saw the 1.8x over x86. Jensen: x86 CPUs, the hyperscale CPUs, were designed to be rented. And so you want as many CPU cores as possible, because the economics of CPUs in the last generation was: what's the dollars per core.

In this new world, AI doesn't rent cores. AI generates tokens, and they sell tokens. And so your fundamental purpose is to go through that exchange, go through that loop as fast as you can, and generate tokens as fast as you can.

Lex: The more you buy, the more you make. You might be the best salesman in the world. [laughter] Jensen: It's easy. It's not a complicated thing. The technology is complicated, but the business model is — Lex: Amazing, amazing, amazing. [laughter]

签名与同游台湾

Jensen: All right, Lex. You got to sign here. "Lex was here, too." Lex: Yeah, all right. [laughter] Jensen: The great Lex Fridman. Lex: Yes. The love I'm getting from here is incredible. Jensen: No, he didn't happen to be here. He flew out to hang out. We're going to hang out for a couple days. I'm going to show him Taiwan. Fan: Awesome podcast. Very long ones. [laughter] Lex: Very, very long. Jensen: And you learn a lot, learn a lot. Lex: And learn a lot, and learn a lot. Thank you.

五层蛋糕与街头小吃

Jensen: AI is a five-layer cake. I think I'll have that one. Lex have — Lex: I think I have the — I have that the green one. Jensen: Did you enjoy some good food? Lex: Yeah. That street food is insane. [laughter] Jensen: This is good. This is a conference cake.

登台与"甲壳虫式"的玩笑

Host: Now, let's welcome Jensen and all our Computex executives on the stage. We're going to take one last group — Lex: Jensen Huang is like the Beatles in the '60s. Jensen: Except the Beatles actually had talent. Lex: Yeah, right. Well, I saw you dance on stage. It was all right. It was pretty good. [laughter] That wasn't quite John Travolta talent. [cheering] Remember that? Oh my goodness. Jensen: This is one of the best. I have so many happy memories of that.

SK Hynix 与 LPDDR4

Host: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to SK Hynix — trillion-dollar company. No wonder supply so tight. Memory so big. You want to see something? Jensen: SK Hynix, legendary high bandwidth memory company. SK Hynix rep: We invented this — LPDDR4 memory into data centers. Twice the bandwidth, half the power. Jensen: And now, please make more. SK Hynix rep: Yeah, yeah. Please make more.

Wabi-sabi 时刻

Jensen: Oh, look at that. That's beautiful. You know, when I was young, I would think that that's not good. But now, I love wabi-sabi. You know, beautiful things — [don't need to] be perfect. Yeah. I love that. Lex: Imperfection is beauty. Jensen: Yeah, look at that. One of a kind.

老一代 GPU 的致敬

Lex: That's my favorite part — is all the different GPUs that people [bring], the old-school ones, all the old-school 1080, the Titan RTX — Jensen: 1080 generation. Titan. [cheering] You know, I've seen this on TV. [cheering] We're brothers. We're brothers. Lex: Yeah, we're brothers. Jensen: All right, we'll take it. Lex: Pretty good? Jensen: It's nice to have just a — I love this guy.

机械键盘与声控未来

Jensen: Oh, I love these keyboards. Lex, try this. Fan: Lex, mechanical? Lex: Oh god, they're the best. Jensen: Oh, nice. Lex: Look how delightful they feel. This — real joy. Jensen: I have bad news for you. Lex: Oh. Jensen: [In the] future, it's mostly going to be voice controlled. Lex: I think so, yeah. I think — better typing, do you? Jensen: Yeah, yeah. I have a hard time thinking when I'm just talking. Speed is not everything. Sometimes you have to pause and think. Look at that. Back to the '80s. Look at this. Thank you, brother.

收尾

Host: Ladies and gentlemen, Lex Fridman. Lex: Dàjiā hǎo.

item.title: [Odds on Open] Hedge Fund Manager Joseph Walsh: Always Play Weaker Players
item.dc:creator: Odds on Open
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：他其实在"反向使用"扑克——不是赢得牌局，而是选择不去的牌桌

大多数人读到"扑克手优势"会立刻想到：读心、心理战、虚张声势、GTO 策略。但 Walsh 几乎完全不谈这些。他承认自己"甚至没进过前百分位"，却靠扑克赚到钱——靠的是选桌而不是打牌。

这里藏着一个被整个投资行业系统性忽视的真相：绝大多数"选股方法论"书籍都在教你如何打牌，但顶级 Alpha 来自于拒绝坐上某些牌桌。 他对冲基金的核心框架不是"我能比谁更聪明"，而是"在哪个时间尺度上、哪个流动性区间里，聪明人已经退场了？" 他明确说：3-6 个月视角的欧洲工业股——那是多策略平台的屠宰场，不去；流动性 1000-3000 万美元/日的名字——他们因杠杆约束进不来，所以我去。

这是一种负向定义的 edge：不是"我强在哪"，而是"对手弱在哪、或根本不来"。换个说法——他的 Alpha 不是技能溢价，而是结构性缺席套利。

二、跨领域连接：Walsh 的"时间尺度套利"与生态学的"生态位分化"是同一个数学结构

生物学里有个 Gause 竞争排斥原理：两个物种若占据完全相同的生态位，必有一个灭绝。于是进化的真正故事不是"更强"，而是生态位分化——猫头鹰夜间捕食、鹰白天捕食，同一片森林两种生物共存。

Walsh 本能地做了同样的事。多策略平台在 1-6 个月时间尺度 × 10M+ 流动性 × 低 beta 约束的生态位里是顶级掠食者。他没有正面硬刚，而是迁移到了另一个生态位：12+ 个月视角 × 小流动性池 × 可承受集中度。这不是"我更擅长投资"，而是"我吃不同的食物"。

更有意思的推论：随着多策略平台 AUM 持续膨胀，它们的生态位反而在收窄——杠杆越高，可投品种越受流动性限制。Walsh 的生态位因此在被动扩大。这解释了一个反直觉现象：对冲基金行业越拥挤，专注"非主流时间尺度"的小基金 edge 越大，而不是越小。市场效率不是均匀上升的，它是在特定生态位里上升、在其他生态位里下降。

三、最被低估的那句话："早期 Alpha 是最好的 Alpha"——它暗示了一个心理学的残酷真相

他轻描淡写地说："从 100 涨到 500 和从 500 涨到 1000 都是 100% 收益，但在电子表格上看不出前者比后者好得多。"

这不是技术分析话术。这是在说：人类的大脑系统性低估了"确定性的隐藏成本"。 后期上涨看起来"更安全"是因为叙事更清晰、共识更强——但清晰的叙事恰恰是风险溢价消失的标志。你以 500 买入 Palantir 比以 100 买入感觉更安全，但按风险调整后收益看，感觉越安全的交易，边际 Alpha 越低。

跨领域连接——这正是认知科学里的"解释深度错觉"（Illusion of Explanatory Depth）：一件事被反复解释，大脑把"熟悉"误认成"理解"，把"理解"误认成"低风险"。市场把这种错觉定价化了：当一个故事被反复讲述、被 CNBC 嘉宾口若悬河地解释，PE 扩张就是在为这种集体错觉付费。

所以 Walsh 的真正方法论不是"买早"，而是"卖早"。 他承认几乎每次都卖得太早。但这不是缺陷——这是他的核心风控：在市场把你的洞见"叙事化"之前离场。因为一旦故事被广泛接受，你的 Alpha 就从"信息差"变成了"情绪差"——而情绪差是他明确说不想和多策略平台/散户竞争的那个战场。

一个让人汗毛直立的推论：今天你最有信心的那只 AI 股票，可能正是你 Alpha 最低的那只。 不是因为它基本面变差了，而是因为你对它的"确信感"本身，就是集体叙事成熟的信号。

📝 转录文本

Hedge Fund Manager Joseph Walsh: Always Play Weaker Players

开场

Ethan: Your returns are great. Sortino over two, 60% annualized.

What are the advantages associated with being a great poker player for investing? Do you like to buy on the way up or buy on the way down? The expected value of buying a stock at 100 on a certain day and 100 on a different day, they're not the same.

What great returns look like are high compounding with no blow ups. That's the holy grail.

Joe, thank you so much for coming on the pod.

Joe: Ethan, thank you for having me and congrats on the success and growth of your show.

一、扑克手的优势：缺失信息博弈与风险管理

Ethan: What are the advantages associated with being a great poker player for investing?

Joe: I think so i'm not an active poker player nowadays but i take a lot from my time as a younger man uh playing the game and i think you know there's a particularly on the trading side you know pure investing and you know maybe there are fewer parallels but in the trading side of the business there are several transferable skill sets where great poker players naturally would have some advantage at also being good at trading.

So one of those would be that they're effectively both games of missing information. So, you know, in poker, you have 52 cards, you have certain variables that are constrained. In the game of No Limit Hold'em, you would be dealt two cards. So you now know there are 50 remaining cards in the deck. You have card removal effects as cards are dealt on the board. You know, there's more card removal effects. You know, every single one of these pieces of information affects the odds of certain hands being made. And also, there's so many variables in that game, but it basically transcends really well across the arena of trading.

风险管理：赢家还要避免成为输家

I think great poker players ultimately are very good risk managers. There are people who are very winning poker players, but they never make it to the top of that arena because their risk management isn't good enough and they're able to generate huge wins, but they're not able to preserve capital as a great hedge fund manager needs to preserve capital as they're stalking the next asymmetric investment in their portfolio.

So it's not enough to be a winner. You also have to avoid being a loser effectively and great poker players who have generated long, durable careers, if you could call playing poker a career, which, you know, for the very best, they've managed to carve that out for themselves, they all have that very disciplined bankroll management.

市场效率与学习的赛跑

They study very hard, which the greatest investors and greatest traders do because they understand that market efficiency as a function of time goes up. I've seen that in my time in markets for the last 14 years. When I came in, stocks were often in the markets I was investing and trading in, they were way wrong. Those gaps close over time, but as you get better, your ability to monetize those situations and spot them earlier increases. So you basically have to increase your edge faster than the market becomes efficient for your edge to grow.

Game Selection：始终对阵更弱的玩家

And yeah, aside from studying to improve and managing risk, capital, or in a poker vernacular, your bankroll well, great poker players are usually also very good at game selection. So, be making sure that, you know, if you're risking money against other players or in a trading situation, you know, it might be market making at a huge firm versus market making at another huge firm. You always, the basic premise is you always want to make sure you're up against weaker players.

So myself, I wouldn't say I was the world's gift to poker, far from it. I'm not even in the top percentiles or whatever. I was not a great player, but I had great results. And that was mainly because at least within the areas of bankroll management, and being able to select good games and things like that, I did a good enough job, not a world-class job, but I did a good enough job that I was able to generate really good returns.

And yeah, I mean, that was a long time ago, but I carry a lot of those lessons and particularly the mathematics and statistics of, you know, expected value, variance, these dominate my thinking in terms of how I appraise any random variable, how I look at the world. It's quite probabilistic. So hopefully that gives you a general framework on some of the key skills and how it's so transferable to the markets.

二、投资中的 Game Selection：避开最聪明的对手

Ethan: On game selection and how great poker players are able to pick good games, I'd love to hear about how that weaves into your process.

Joe: Yeah, thanks for the kind words. Yeah, I could have been taking a huge amount of risk, but I guess the Sortino statistic you calculated covers that. But yeah, the answer to how I think about, I guess, game selection to borrow that is you want to be in stocks, in sectors and in markets where you basically are in anti-competitive situations where different pools of capital have different agendas. You're not against the most talented investors.

被动投资与多策略平台如何重塑市场结构

There are lots of market forces and market structure that's probably good to visit at this moment in terms of understanding what drives pricing and inefficiency. So there's been huge growth in passive investing. There's been huge growth in AUM inside of multi-strategy hedge funds.

And passive investing is largely a price indiscriminate buyer or seller of an asset. where it's payroll linked and employment linked at the end of the month, someone gets their check and a certain portion of it via a pension deduction or otherwise goes into the BlackRock ETF that the pension fund manager has decided upon. I'm oversimplifying, but you get the point. There's no discerning of which stock is the best stock. It's just whatever's in that ETF is getting bought at that moment, regardless of value.

So I think most people understand that and the growth of that from being 6% of flows to over like half of flows is really material in terms of, I guess, how stocks get priced because effectively just by definition, you do get a misallocation of capital because where ETFs are market cat weighted, the big receive more and you get it's basically a momentum trade. Things that have gone up, get more inflows, things that have gone down, get less. And so you get a perpetuation of that.

Where you have an increasing share of AUM being run in equity books at up to eight times GMV, in fixed income books, you know, greater than 10 times GMV, sometimes up to 15 times. And this is all available by PB data and industry surveys. And then allocators are allocating into these platforms under SMAs, using leverage from their prime broker accounts, they're ultimately volatility targeting and they're very good. They're some of the best firms in the world at delivering like volatility targeted returns. So they're good at delivering cash plus equity returns with a desirable sharp, whether that be like 1.5 net to the client after fees. But, you know, internally they gross at a higher sharp than that. But the product is volatility targeting, it's not profit maximizing. So they're always running on a centralized risk limit with stops, factor constrained, beta constrained.

时间尺度与赛道选择

And so tying all of these factors back into game selection and picking stocks, I think the first thing I think about is time horizon. I don't want to be looking at a security and valuing it on a three to six month timeframe where I'm competing against another very well resourced, motivated man or woman who is working inside of one of these firms that has got way better corporate access, has got way better access to short term information, proprietary data sets.

And whilst a ton of this has been democratized, particularly in this current AI moment, and so the playing field is being leveled and it's actually a wonderful time to be a smaller investor or be running a smaller fund, the fact is, is you've got to pick your time horizons to be avoiding very good players, you've got to pick your sectors where all of the pods who used to do that have been shut down and all of the investors have given up. And you typically get that in cyclical sectors, but whatever it looks like, the game selection aspect is running away from competition. And that's where greater inefficiency by definition lives.

And there are huge pockets of that in the equity market today. So time horizon is a big one. If you think you're going to have a huge edge trading European industrials on a three month timeframe, trying to have a better view on earnings and the delta between market value and earnings, I would politely disagree with most people that they wouldn't have an edge there. But for ourselves, we have huge edge in timeframes that are greater than 12 months in different sectors and different markets where it's just not as competitive.

And that can be for reasons of it's not worth these people's time when they're running 100 billion of capital levered multiple times to muck around in names that have got liquidity of 10, 20, $30 million a day. It's just the liquidity constraint might be unattractive for them, but the capacity with which I could run money is very attractive to single digit billions and still have a huge edge and still remain very liquid.

So hopefully that gives you a sense of some of the things that drive decision making when it comes to thinking about where to look and where great returns might lie and the time horizon over which they could be extracted.

But that would not be the norm and you know my hit rate in those situations is very good but they don't come up often.

So uh you know but to answer your question in the spirit in which it was asked um where things are exceptional uh you know you definitely you it's a big mistake to be gun shy and not take an appropriately sized position because truthfully in a given year, it's multifaceted because there are many of these situations that you might not be able to spot them all. They might be outside your circle of competence. You might not understand them. So it's like an overlap of a Venn diagram between your circle of competence, familiarity, ability to price a security really well and better than the market and the market overlapping on the other side of the Venn diagram with giving you that opportunity.

So that intersection is not as big for most investors, unfortunately, as they'd like to believe. And so those moments where you can truly, you know, really deploy disproportionately large amounts of capital in a safe and responsible way relative to what your normal sizing would be is just, you know, arithmetically at a lower frequency.

九、不可动摇的规则：空头风控

Ethan: Are there any rules that you stick to as like a hard stop as in i know you mentioned that you have principles you have views on how to enter how to exit parts of your process but that you're always evolving is there anything right now that you think this is the way i'm going to this is one particular part of my process i will stick to no matter what um and if there is something like that what is it?

Joe: Yeah, for sure. I mean, there's tons of rules and rules, you know, you develop them over time, you improve them. I mean, I think we probably conceptually discussed a lot more aspects of framework towards investing on the long side than the short.

做空的数学决定了更严风控

And I think in terms of risk management, there is just a necessity to have tighter risk control on the short side. That starts immediately with sizing. I size shorts far, far smaller than, you know, I would size a typical long. You know, you told me you studied maths. I studied maths. I mean, the maths and the mathematics of shorting you know, just dictate that it's a high risk activity. It's not that it's not accreted to performance. It's not that when it's done well and you're very good at borrowing that you can, you know, do it in a way that's secretive to returns and in many instances risk reducing. But, you know, the risk is elevated just on an apples for apples basis. Your payoff is capped. Your losses are potentially infinite as the inversion of the long payoff and the economics and the cost of carry of a short position is also just typically higher net of borrow cost, dividend yield, etc.

So, yeah, I mean, there are very hard limits that I have in place on the short side. I'm definitely far stricter in terms of risk control on the short book than the long book. But, you know, I have a ton of risk control in the long book as well.

投机 vs 投资：价格是不是你的止损？

You know, it's ultimately driven by the fundamentals. And just going back to an example, where you're in a situation where there's a high degree of operating leverage, a high degree of financial leverage. If things don't go well, that's an equity that can go to zero clearly. And the debt can overwhelm the equity and the creditors take over the company.

So, you know, if you were, you know, in a large position in such a situation and you weren't using last traded price as a stop loss, at a certain level, at a certain point, if operations are deteriorating, the results of the business are bad, I would go as far as to say you're not investing anymore, you're gambling. And that's not the business we're in.

So, so i think you know the the rules are very important and you know on a security by security basis it's very important to establish before you put that position on what your risk is again it goes to underwriting that downside because you know different stocks have very different downside potentials they have very different upside potentials and you know you can only really fill in the blanks on those missing pieces of information by doing a ton of work and going through and understanding what the earnings potential is, what the assets are worth. Is this a franchise that hardens as it pays? Or is this a franchise that consumes its assets as it pays out shareholders? That's a common framework that we're analyzing longs and shorts against and what's left for shareholders at the end.

So, yeah, hopefully that gives you a sense. But, yeah, on the short side in particular, we have several rules. I won't go into them for the purposes of this call, but, you know, there is strict risk control for sure.

圣杯：高复利 + 零爆仓

Because ultimately, at the end of the day, what great returns look like are, you know, high compounding with no blowups. That's the holy grail. And the only way you can avoid those blow-ups is with good risk control. So if you're not controlling a risk, as some of my friends joke, if you get caught speeding, eventually it's going to catch up with you. So yeah, you have to have very disciplined risk control.

十、市场参与者结构变化下的常见错误

Ethan: So the conversation, talk a little bit about EV, making bets, longs, sizing. The market's changed a lot. And the you talked about active, passive, talked about the pods, retail, and those seem to be real drivers of price that fundamental all managers need to study, but fundamental managers all managers need to study. Are there any mistakes that you think a lot of investors are making today that stem from a lack of the of understanding of the differences in market participants rather the changes in market participants that have happened in the last call it 10 20 years so that any mistakes I think that people are making today as a result of changing market structure?

Joe: Yeah, I mean, there has to be, right? So what springs to mind is probably people's execution. And we've kind of discussed some of the drivers of that to this point. I think, you know, your execution has to evolve with the way that price evolves. and that you're just, you're doing a better job of controlling risk and improving return by doing that. So if you're still kind of executing the way you were in the year 2000, in the year 2026, you can bet with a very high probability that there's a time slippage that's in your process and leaks that need to be plugged.

新板块是最大的 Edge 来源

I guess more on valuation, people think about valuing assets in different ways, but in the world of equities, it's kind of hard to reinvent the wheel with regards to how you value a company, whether it's a multiples-based valuation, a discounted cash flow-based valuation, a relative transaction valuation.

Where there is definitely room for outsized edge, is where like new sectors come along and no one knows how to value it. So like space was like a great one where, you know, like space as an asset class, you know, it wasn't really a thing 10, 15 years ago. And then you started getting these satellite players and then SpaceX came out of the private markets into the public markets. And you've got this launch asset that's effectively a monopoly.

And obviously within that stock, there is a ton of AI adjacent assets, whether it's XAI or Grok. And if you read the S1, it's all in there. But, but, you know, from the constellation of satellites they're operating within Starlink or, you know, the business they have in launch, you know, I would go as far as to say that most of us are making mistakes in terms of how we try to value that equity because it's new and there's just not the familiarity. There's not the track record.

And so, yeah. For someone who is a specialist in that area, I would argue that there's probably a higher degree of edge on offer because you're going to be competing against people who no less than you, have been through fewer cycles than you.

So, yeah, as that sector grows and more businesses come to market, that's an area clearly where people are probably more likely to make mistakes than not, to answer your question. Where sectors are very competitive and you've got, you know, 15 pods in London and 30 pods in New York, all pricing the same 10 stocks that have been listed on the market for 30 years. And, you know, the edges are so thin. I don't think people are making big mistakes there. I think that's a very competitive field and if you're going to sit down and try and take those people on, you need to be very, very good. And that is not what I'm trying to do. I don't have to have a view on those names running a concentrated portfolio and I can make fantastic returns by avoiding it completely.

So, yeah, people will hopefully make new mistakes. They won't make the same mistakes. And as the markets change and new sectors come along and market structure changes, all of that changes. But, yeah, I'd say that's a good broad church of my current thinking on that.

十一、Tesla、Palantir、与"早期 Alpha"

Ethan: What you mentioned about names changing where people not understanding how to fairly value something being very interesting. That stood out to me, especially, I mean, I'm thinking of a time I remember in 2020, there's an investor I deeply respected and he was talking about his Tesla long. And I was asking him, what's the reason for the long? And he said, there's so much money in the system and there's no way to fairly value this company.

And so even and I think like that sentiment, I mean, clearly extremely well timed. But I can see the flip side of that, where in some sense, a lot of it is timing sentiment, especially for something like that, because Tesla clearly year over year is traded kind of sideways up a lot, sometimes down a lot.

What do you think about purely buying names or picking names based off of those narratives, based off of sentiment, will you ever bet on exclusively multiple expansion? Or does it feed into other things as well? I'd love to hear your thoughts.

Joe: Okay. A tough assignment, but I'll give it my best shot. So your framework there from that investor you spoke to, I'm guessing we've emerged from the March 2020 liquidation. Powell has begun the $4 trillion expansion of the balance sheet. And that investor was screening for equities that would perform very well in a rich liquidity environment. And they somewhat correctly identified Tesla. And I'd say very correctly, probably because the stock probably did brilliantly.

I guess where they say it's hard to value the company, that's just kind of outside of my framework because you know, the bears in that situation would say, well, it's a very expensive auto company, but six years hence, obviously, you know, to an extent with RoboTaxi, which has become extraordinarily competitive, you know, a lot of people are now arguing that that company is effectively a single product bet on Optimus and his focus is elsewhere in SpaceX and in other ventures, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah.

But would I bet that on effectively just multiple expansion? No, is the answer. Because, you know, so much of the process is based on understanding more than just that. It's, you know, that's it's a linear single factor, which is an explainer of a return, but there are many more explanatory variables to the return than just the multiple.

Palantir：基本面 + 流动性拐点

So, yeah. I think I definitely understand the concept though, in that Tesla is somewhat of a concept stock and it's a bit of a cult. And so this is a name that's going to be a disproportionate recipient of flows in a rising liquidity environment. And can it go from 25 times to 100 times? Sure. Because in a PE expansion environment, you know, if it's 50, why not 60? If it's 60, why not 70? And there are people who trade those markets really well.

I think for myself, you know, there are certain stocks in that environment where I did position in quite aggressively. And, you know, very early on, Palantir was one. So, the chat GPT, I mean, this was further along, obviously. I mean, this was more after November 22, chat GPT came out, but there was a similar bottoming in the liquidity cycle at that moment. And I'm just using Polanza as an example, because it kind of rhymes in my head with Tesla in terms of one of these stocks that became a cult.

And, you know, whilst the earnings are there and the cash flow is there, you know, was kind of conceptual at the start because there was some aspects of the operating activity is classified and your disclosures aren't great in certain aspects of the business, etc. Obviously, it's improved over time. But effectively, you had the dominant AI business at the time, you know, when you were looking for percentage of revenues dedicated to AI in large liquid names, there was a long tail in the market of kind of stocks and companies that had just put AI in their ticker, but they weren't legitimate AI companies.

And just by observing the market, I kind of obviously very aware of Peter Thiel as an investor and someone who founded that company alongside Karp. It was a direct listing, came to market just before then in that paradigm. And there was a situation where obviously after the bear market in 2022, you had a bottoming in the liquidity side for the Q4 2022, where if you remember February that year, Putin had invaded Ukraine. Powell was raising rates at the fastest pace in recorded history from effectively the lower bound up towards 5%. So there's a very kind of short, sharp pullback in the markets and those richly valued concept stocks got buried.

But at that moment where OpenAI released ChatGPT in November 2022, and you could see the usage just rocketing, and within weeks and months, everyone would say, "Oh, I'll just ChatGPT it." And the narrative, to give you an example of the narratives you were talking about, is everyone was saying, "Oh, when the product becomes a verb, and it's your favorite app on your phone, you know you're off to the races." And people were saying these kind of things back then.

But with Palantir, you actually had a business that was net cash, had billions of dollars of AI-specific revenues at that time. They had a government and commercial business. The commercial business was much smaller back then. But it was growing very quickly, clearly accelerating, and estimates weren't capturing that. But as an analyst, I was struggling with the lack of disclosure. And there was a lot of red flags. It was very high stock-based comp, which is common in software companies and particularly in the Valley in America. But it was elevated.

And so, you know, I did what I've commonly done where I identified something early and sold early, but made a very good return. But it was all based on fundamentals. There was a lot of free cash flow generation into a valuation that made it attractive on an EV to free cash flow basis. When I was buying the company at a 20 billion EV, you know, again, against the forecast I was able to generate, the business was extremely attractively valued. And I definitely sold it far too early. But I guess as Rothschild famously said, you can make a fortune or he said, I've made a fortune by selling things too early.

早期 Alpha vs 晚期 Alpha

And just on that point, Ethan, I think something that doesn't come out in spreadsheets is that like the alpha in situations is different. So if you have someone who generates 100% in a situation and it's a stock that goes from price of 100 to price of 1000 and they get the last bit, the kind of run from 500 to 1000. That is the riskiest part of the move before the stock tops, but it doesn't jump out on a spreadsheet. You know, it's the risk premium that's attached from the early alpha.

The early alpha is the best alpha, in my opinion, because it's where the valuations are lowest, the risks to equity are the lowest. And so even though it doesn't jump out when two people have made 100%, those returns can be extremely different. And the amount of risk that was taken, even if you're not looking in financial leverage terms, just fundamental valuation terms, and on a per share risk per unit of return.

Yeah, I generally try to be sizing larger where on a valuation basis, you're early in the move and then I'm pulling capital out as expected values declining as the equity is rising. And yeah, that way you're able to protect capital a lot easier. So as expected value goes up, as the expected value comes down and variance of return is going up as a stock is appreciating, very quickly pulling the capital back.

十二、AI 大交易的当下格局

Ethan: I think the only obvious question from there is what are your thoughts on the AI trade as it stands today?

Joe: No, I'm not sure. I mean, I see lots of risks. Things I'm thinking about are that from a regulatory perspective, there's a lot of concern on cybersecurity risk. There are increasing incidents taking place, which the companies are volunteering, whether it's the Hugging Face incident or there is some, there's a spectrum of, I guess we could call them mishaps.

But it's kind of undeniable at this point that whether you like it or not, you are exposed to this thematic in today's market because, you know, a statistic I read recently was that 40% of S&P earnings are now explicit or derived from AI. If you look in the credit markets as a percentage of issuance, whether it's the bonds from Meta or Google or SoftBank who hit the headlines two days ago, issuing a very high yielding bonds. AI is very represented in the credit markets now.

And yeah, I mean, there's a bear case, there's a base case, and there's a bull case. And each of them is going to have disproportionate risk for the market.

房东策略：数据中心 REIT 的低风险角度

I think I think what we think about is the sustainability of the capex that these hyperscalers are able to deploy and how you can participate in that as an equity investor without taking silly amounts of risk. So there are listed securities that are selling into this where you could be a landlord of a data center with a contract where you retain first liens on the property, your capex per megawatt is capped, the client is taking a ton of the risk, and you're effectively a landlord trading at a yield on cost in the teens, and there appears that are REITs or otherwise that are trading at cap rates in the single digits. And those are very attractively priced situations. And without naming them, unfortunately, I'm not able to give you those while we're trading them.

But yeah, I mean, we are active in the space in equities where we can see a very good return without taking a ton of risk.

OpenAI/Anthropic 的脆弱性

I mean, in terms of the cash flow burn and the financial position of these lease commitments on a take or pay basis, I think, you know, people are going to be keenly reading these S1s when they come out. You know, if these companies execute to the ball case and revenue keeps growing, they're going to be in a position to satisfy these obligations. And they're going to be very, very, very valuable companies. I'm speaking here mainly about OpenAI and Anthropic.

But to the extent you've got very high cash burn, very high obligations that aren't on balance sheet yet, that will come on balance sheet as that critical IT load is delivered, uh there is there is an outcome where the financial position becomes yeah uh fragile let's let's put it like that.

So uh you know ai as a technology is phenomenal uh we use it every day it's been extremely helpful to our process you know i don't i'm not one of these doomers who you know things it doesn't add value or things it's like redundant i think it's transformational.

分解 AI 价值链

But the actual, as a consumer of the product and then being an investor of the businesses is a completely different proposition. And, you know, accretion to equity value through that entire value chain, where at the top on the GPU side, you've got Nvidia. On the frontier lab side, you've got OpenAI Anthropic and a host of others beneath them that you alluded to in the private markets as well. The kind of Neo cloud space, you've got, the nebbiases, the coolweaves, the iris energies. In the Powered Shell players, you've got a host of listed players, or you've got fully fledged REITs like Equinix, Digital Realty. There's a host of these previously Bitcoin miners that have migrated over to AI, high performance compute. Then you've got memory.

So this is a very large value chain. It's a very large industry structure. And, you know, the whole thing sums to, you know, easily north of 20, 30 trillion of market cap. And it's a very, very big trade. And I think it's going to be very dangerous for the market if it doesn't work out.

供给侧瓶颈：吉瓦与 NIMBY

And I guess analyzing demand is one thing, but something we do a lot of is analyzing supply as well. And if you look at the gigawatts that are forecast to come into the market, even in the U.S. market, if you just look at the top five states, so like markets like Virginia, Texas, Pennsylvania, California, there's been a lot of headlines recently about it's becoming a political issue because you're running into nimbyism. People don't want a gigawatt monstrosity in their backyard.

You know, to the extent that permitting becomes an issue, like you saw in New York, there was a pause and, you know, permitting's been halted, perhaps indefinitely, we'll have to see. You know, there's discussions in ERCOT right now in Texas. There are lots of state elections happening. This is a big political football that people are kicking around. And if it wins votes, you know, politicians are going to campaign on it.

And that creates risk to consensus, because if the market is pricing that there's 200 gigawatt speed being delivered next year and that number misses by 25 percent, the earnings are going to miss accordingly for lack of delivered infrastructure.

芯片世代与冷却约束

So, very bullish on the technology and its potential. The trade has become incredibly large, even if there is risk to earnings and there's other technological aspects like something that is happening as Nvidia comes out with these generations of new chips is that the cooling requirements from thermal power design or thermal design power, which is effectively the amount of watts that are required or emitted from the chip and required for cooling.

So you've gone from like Hopper to Blackwell to Rubin, Rubin Ultra, and then you've got Fineman coming after that, which should be the next generation. And just the chips are so much more powerful. And, you know, there is the amount of packages put in per chip rises, the amount of heat that they're emitting goes up. And so, you know, ultimately NVIDIA has, you know, developed a low power mode as a just in case for this being delivered.

But there are many cooling solutions that are being worked through in the market right now, but they're not there yet. And that's another form of risk. It's like, well, you could be building these world class chips at the frontier and ultimately, you may go from single-phase cooling via liquid cooling to cooling in-chip, which may then become an NVIDIA product.

技术乐观 + 结构警惕：ASML 的类比

So there are so many technological risks. There are regulatory risks. There are permitting risks. But the truth is that the potential of the technology is so big. And people said these things about ASNL like 10, 15 years ago. They were like, EUV lithography will never work. And Nikken and Canon and the others just fell away and ASML kept betting on it. They made the breakthrough and it's the most valuable company in Europe today.

So the potential is there, but there's a lot of risk. And our job as investors is to dissect that value chain, understand all the technology constraints, regulatory, political, etc. and then find the most asymmetric attractive part of the value chain, both long and short, and position accordingly.

十三、言行不一致：隐藏的 AI 多头

Ethan: Yeah, I mean, what's also so funny about AI, not really funny, but just it's a cool fact, is that you'll have these people or, you know, an example is, say, a college student. And he watches something on YouTube and he says, "AI is a bubble, AI is a bubble." But his career, the way he's recruiting, the bets he's making with his personal decisions are all extremely correlated to the AI factor. Or people who make calls about, say, the US, another example, and then with their careers are extremely long the US. It's like these incongruencies that I find very funny.

十四、最大的个人 Edge：产业结构研究

Ethan: And I guess final question, talked about a lot during this podcast. Out of all the parts of your process, what would you say is the most important that lots of other hedge fund managers, lots of other investors could learn from?

Joe: I think it's a pretty self-aggrandizing question. I'm not sure I could teach these you know, great fund managers much, but I think probably if I could twist your wording slightly where I think my process maybe has a large amount of edge, if you allow it, is I think the work that we do on industry structure yields a lot of alpha.

AI 价值链例证

I guess I'll give you a couple of examples to bring it to life because it's just more fun when you bring it down to a stock. So we just went through some of the AI value chain there. So starting at the very top, you've got chip manufacturers, you've got like Nvidia, you've got the TSMCs, you've got the AMDs, the Intels and all those people. You've got then in memory, you've got Micron, Samsung Hynix. On the lab side, you've got OpenAI, Anthropic, a host of others. In the Neo cloud space, you've got the CoreWaves, the Nebiuses, the Iris Energies, etc. And then going back through PowerShell, you've then got a host of data sensor providers. There's four different products even within that.

And to cover like 50 names, and you don't have to go into molecular detail, but you do have to understand their business model. You do have to understand their position in the value chain, how much of the industry's profit accrues to them, and then how industry structure can change over time so that their share of the profit may go up or down, their share of the revenue and cash may go up or down. What is that industry growing at? So are these, is this pocket of the industry taking market share or losing it?

And so, yeah, an area I was quite early to was the PowerShell players within the AI value chain. You could buy those businesses on enterprise values of $1 million per megawatt on their secured power portfolios. And they're trading you know at three to four having gone to seven to eight at peak and the good ones did more than that. I'm giving you like sector statistics.

风电案例：Cadeler 与价值链转移

So yeah, I think doing industry understanding industry structure as a stock picker an equity investor and a buyer or seller of companies is very valuable, but it's very time consuming, which is why a lot of people don't do it. And I understand that, but there is a big ROI on that work.

You know, another one, I mean, there's several really, where industry structure has led to not just an individual great opportunity, but great long, short opportunities. A few years ago, it was in the wind space, where you effectively have developers who are the owner-operators of wind farms. You have the turbine makers who provide the equipment that goes into those wind farms. You have cable manufacturers that are manufacturing the export cable that goes from the substation onshore out to this offshore wind farm. You have the turbine installation vessels, you know, that ultimately are these fleets of self-propelled jack-off vessels that jack down on the seabed. They have a Hussmann crane attached to them. They're phenomenal assets and they're very bespoke. You know, you can't replace it and retrofit an oil rig to do this work.

And, you know, there's a company in particular that I used to be a shareholder of called Cadala, which by taking out an entity we were long of became, frankly, a monopolist of this profit pool and disproportionately attracted economics relative to the rest of the industry at a very, very low starting valuation.

So, yeah. So yeah, we, you know, through the evolution of this industry over time, back in 2017, everyone in the wind space was making very attractive returns because they were being remunerated on a feed-in tariff basis. And then there was a pivot to auction, which basically drove a lot more competitive pricing. That led to more competitive bids from developers. They pushed that deflation down into the value chain. So pricing per turbine per megawatt came down. And then they pushed that through their supply chain. Everyone got squeezed and the economics were terrible.

You know, the business effectively went from generating low double digit operating margins and making good returns to having some very lean years and having multiple profit warnings. Meanwhile, Cadla was sat there filling up a backlog and their share price did extraordinarily well.

But it's understanding how all those parts of the industry speak to each other and not just looking at one in isolation saying, "Okay, this is growing, it's cheap, I'm going to buy some." If you know how all those moving parts talk to each other and you're meeting all of those companies at conferences and you're doing the work, you can you can have a far better kind of ability to to cover risks that can be coming and also see upsides before other people see them.

So probably that's the thing that's been the most helpful. And yeah, it's it's a lot of work, but it's it's worth it understand and the structure of industries there's alpha there.

结束

Ethan: Thank you Joe for coming on the pod. This was awesome.

Joe: Ethan, thank you and uh yeah well done on the growth of the show. I've uh I've got value from the episodes and hopefully I've given a bit of value back so yeah well done.

Ethan: Absolutely man, thank you.

item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：他其实在"反向使用"扑克——不是赢得牌局，而是**选择不去的牌桌**
大多数人读到"扑克手优势"会立刻想到：读心、心理战、虚张声势、GTO 策略。但 Walsh 几乎完全不谈这些。他承认自己"甚至没进过前百分位"，却靠扑克赚到钱——**靠的是选桌而不是打牌**。
这里藏着一个被整个投资行业系统性忽视的真相：**绝大多数"选股方法论"书籍都在教你如何打牌，但顶级 Alpha 来自于拒绝坐上某些牌桌。** 他对冲基金的核心框架不是"我能比谁更聪明"，而是"**在哪个时间尺度上、哪个流动性区间里，聪明人已经退场了？**" 他明确说：3-6 个月视角的欧洲工业股——那是多策略平台的屠宰场，不去；流动性 1000-3000 万美元/日的名字——他们因杠杆约束进不来，所以我去。
这是一种**负向定义的 edge**：不是"我强在哪"，而是"**对手弱在哪、或根本不来**"。换个说法——他的 Alpha 不是技能溢价，而是**结构性缺席套利**。
## 二、跨领域连接：Walsh 的"时间尺度套利"与生态学的"生态位分化"是同一个数学结构

💡 创造性洞见

从"旁观者"到"行动者"：代理商务的本体论转变

Terry 用了一个极其克制但意义深远的词：代理从 spectator 变成了 actor，而让这个转变成立的不是智能提升，而是一张能支付的卡。这是整个访谈最被低估的洞察——智能并不等于能动性，能动性来自于"能让你损失钱"的权力。一个能推荐却不能付款的 AI 本质上和一本百科全书没有区别；而一旦它能从你账户中划出资金，它在法律、伦理、经济上都变成了一个新物种。这意味着整个"AGI 什么时候到来"的辩论可能走错了路——AGI 的真正门槛不是 benchmark 分数，而是支付凭证的信任边界。有趣的跨界联系：这与"法人"的诞生惊人相似。现代公司之所以成为公司，不是因为它有多聪明，而是因为它能签合同、能被起诉、能持有财产。代理商务正在悄悄地让 AI 获得类似"法人"的功能性人格。

拉斯维加斯三步验证法：代理时代最被忽略的债务

Alex 顺手讲的一段"珠宝店-拉斯维加斯"类比值得单独放大。传统交易验证有三步：卡是真的吗？人是卡主吗？人神志清醒吗？ 代理商务已经解决了前两步（network tokens + agent registration），但第三步——是否神志清醒——在 AI 语境下变成了"是否幻觉"。而这里有一个几乎没人指出的结构性问题：赌场的"神志清醒"判断由商户承担（没让醉汉付款是商户的责任），但在代理商务里，"幻觉检测"的责任目前完全没有被分配给任何一方。这不是技术缺口，是法律真空。可以预测：未来 12-24 个月，代理公司将不得不像保险公司一样，为自己的"错单"自掏腰包赔付，这会催生一个新品类——代理错误保险（Agent E&O Insurance），并最终把"幻觉率"从一个研究指标变成一个精算指标。

Amazon 封杀 Muse 泄露的秘密：企业对代理的态度，暴露了它真正是什么

这是整段对话里最有爆点但两人都轻描淡写处理掉的洞察：Amazon 之所以敌视代理，不是因为它是零售商，而是因为它根本不是零售商——它是一家广告公司。代理没有眼球，所以不能被变现。换句话说，一家公司对 AI 代理的接纳程度，是检测它真实商业模式的试剂。热情拥抱的（Shopify 下的 SMB）靠商品差价赚钱；犹豫的（Walmart）既靠差价也靠流量和会员订阅；敌视的（Amazon）主要靠注意力贩卖。这个诊断方法可以反向使用：下一个值得做空的，是那些声称"我们是科技公司"但对代理高度敌对的 SaaS——它们大概率在用"科技"包装"广告"。跨界联系：这与达尔文"检视身体结构即可反推生态位"的做法一模一样——鸟喙的形状暴露它吃什么，公司对代理的 API 政策暴露它真的卖什么。

隐形崩塌：返现、里程、信用卡积分的"保险精算基础"将在三年内瓦解

Terry 几乎是以脚注方式提到了一个会震动整个消费金融行业的事实：信用卡的高额返现之所以存在，是因为"breakage"（破损率）——持卡人错配、遗忘、未优化。而代理恰恰消灭 breakage。一旦我的代理永远给我用对的卡、在对的类目、在对的促销期——那张"餐饮 5% 回赠但其他 1%"的卡在精算上就无法成立。这不是边际调整，这是整个 reward 经济学的塌陷。类比：这与 ETF 对主动管理基金的侵蚀一样——不是击败了对手，而是抽走了对手赖以生存的信息不对称。预测：三年内会出现"反代理化"信用卡产品（例如需要人类生物认证才能解锁高额返现），银行会以"保护用户"为名实际保护自己的毛利。

不对称红利窗口：你现在正站在"2005 年的高频交易员"位置

Alex 自己几乎意识到了但没有点破：早期代理用户正在剥削一个尚未部署代理的世界。所有的"代理帮我省钱"的爽文，都来自于交易对手还在用人类节奏运转。这与 2005 年前后 Renaissance 和 Citadel 面对手工做市商时的处境完全同构——不是因为他们更聪明，而是因为对面还没升级。当 Comcast 也用代理接电话、当航空公司用代理动态定价压制你的升舱代理，这个套利窗口就关闭了。所以现在听这期播客的人，正站在一个历史性窄缝里：你能用代理占便宜的时间，可能只有 18 个月。

Now, one of the things that I think has made VGS a lot more interesting since the days that you first invested — it's been a decade of becoming sort of the most trusted vault online — is that the card networks have also introduced a form of tokenization. Alex: A PAN is a Primary Account Number.

Terry: A PAN is a Primary Account Number.

Alex: — credit card number. It's the 16-digit number that you have on your card.

So VGS as a company vaults all these credentials on behalf of the merchant, also gets all of the network tokens — which is the primary way that these credentials are passed to the payment processor and to the network. And that's what we do today.

从旁观者到行动者：Wallet Wars

Terry: Yeah, I mean — in the last 3 months we've had this huge leap from agents being what I would call spectators to agents being actors. And how do they act on my behalf? Well, if you give them a payment credential in a safe way —

Alex: Right.

Terry: — I can go from recommending the flowers for your wife to buying the flowers for your wife.

And so what's happened with the rise of Muse and Instinct and Town and other AI agents is: once they have access to payment credentials, their utility increases. And so we sort of have kicked off what I kind of call the Wallet Wars, where every wallet is now rushing to connect to the agents.

And of course, as an agent, I want a wallet that has sort of two things: (1) the most number of consumers that already have a credential at that wallet, and (2) a wallet that has a very broad merchant reach. And so right now, this is sort of companies like Stripe Link — they have about 300 million consumers who have an account at Link, about a million merchants use Link. You have Shopify with Shop Pay — similar-ish consumer size, probably more like 1.7 million merchants. Then you have PayPal, which has over 400 million accounts (depends on how that's actually measured), but they have on the order of 30 million merchants. 两种钱包：Apple Pay 式 vs Shop Pay 式

Terry: Yeah. And look, I think the word "wallet" is a bit overused. There's sort of different versions of it.

One is the digital version of your dead-cow wallet, which is that it just stores the payment credential, and when you go to a merchant, you hand that credential to the merchant. That's kind of what Apple Pay does. When I shop with Apple Pay — so when I shop at a store with Apple Pay — Apple is effectively giving my Capital One Visa card, effectively tokenized in the wallet, to the merchant. The merchant receives this credential, and it decides whether it processes it through Chase, or Adyen, or Stripe, or Braintree.

Then you have wallets that actually take care of the transaction for you. So think about Shop Pay, or Link, or PayPal — where the wallet is in fact transacting with me, collecting the money from me, and remitting that back to the merchant.

And what's happening with agentic commerce is we're sort of getting this blend of the two. And it's such a new ecosystem that it actually has parallels for me back to the early days of the internet. For those people who were around in the sort of AOL era: Stripe in many ways is like the AOL of Agentic Commerce. And I mean that as a compliment, in the sense that they've figured out how to make agentic commerce just work in a way that's a very kind of walled-garden approach.

Walmart 枝形吊灯案例：AOL 式方案的边界

Terry: A few examples here would be: if I use Stripe Link, Link's only available at a million merchants. So it's great if the item that I want is available at one of those million merchants. But very often it's available at some place where there isn't a Stripe Link connection.

And I found the lights at Walmart, which makes a ton of sense — Walmart has lots of inventory. And the agent went, loaded the cart, and when it came time to pay, Link didn't have a connection to Walmart. Link has my card, but it can't just give my card over to the agent and over to Walmart.

So, Stripe did something pretty interesting: they purchased the chandeliers on my behalf. They issued their own — this is a Visa virtual card, one-time-use card — made the purchase, and then they charged me, Terry, as a second transaction. This is a little bit how DoorDash works today — you spend a hundred bucks at DoorDash, and then the Dasher goes and pays the restaurant.

But in the case of this Walmart transaction — this is the point about it being the AOL — it worked just great. The item showed up, the transaction went through, I was charged the right amount. But: if there's a problem with the chandelier, typically I call up my bank — Capital One — and I say, "Hey, I had this transaction with Walmart, something went wrong." And they say, "Well, we don't see a Walmart transaction here. We see a Stripe —" "We just see a Stripe transaction."

And in fact — you will find this pretty funny — I know someone who, in the sort of testing phase, did this exact flow on their Amex card, called up Amex, and said, "Hey, this transaction with the merchant didn't go through," but Amex only saw Stripe. So they gave them a phone number to call whoever this Link merchant is. The person called them — it went straight to the cell phone of a Stripe engineer, because Stripe's not set up to run a chargeback.

Visa/Mastercard 为何坚不可摧：Chargeback 的信任机制

Alex: Well, this is the main — one of the reasons why Visa and Mastercard have such impregnable positions is because they intermediate everything, and they set the rules. And chargebacks are very important.

Terry: Yeah.

Alex: Right. Like, what if I paid for something — it's a trust mechanism — I pay you for something, I pay you for lights, you don't deliver the lights. "Oh shoot, I don't have money anymore, what do I do?" No, no, no — you actually have rules by which I can lodge a complaint. And then there's a central intermediary that helps adjudicate those complaints in a way that is more or less fair, that both parties agree on.

I mean, part of the problem — like, this is why crypto cool, but it's kind of a bearer instrument. I pay you with crypto, I'm never getting that back. Which, again, can be a bug or a feature. But for your lights example — like, what if the lights don't work? You want to have Visa and Mastercard in the middle. That's high utility, actually, even for the merchant — because now I am much more willing to buy with the merchant knowing that if they don't actually deliver a product that works, I can get my money back. So that trust mechanism is very important. But again, if you add all these interesting and very clever engineering steps, it just — it doesn't work as well.

开放标准：Agentic Tokens 的到来

Terry: Yeah. So, in fact, this is like, I think, the right sort of direction of travel: from the AOL ecosystem to the open-standards ecosystem.
