item.title: [Latent Space] From Wet Lab to RL Env: 10,000 Drug-Discovery Campaigns in a Weekend — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞见：你的模型可能是个"社会学家"而非"化学家"

Clever Hans（聪明的汉斯）那匹"会算数的马"真正学到的是训练者的微表情——这件 19 世纪的轶事在 Leash Bio 的实验中获得了令人毛骨悚然的现代重演：他们不用任何化学结构，仅用"预测这个分子是谁做的"这个 1,800 维的概率向量作为分子表征，训练出的活性预测模型居然和使用真实化学式的模型表现相当。

这意味着什么？整个计算药物化学领域，可能有相当比例的"SOTA 性能"其实是在学习人类药物化学家的职业偏见——他们选择不做什么、他们崇拜哪些 building block、他们的师承谱系（因为学生会继承导师的"分子口音"）。更惊悚的是：最有预测力的单一特征是分子量——因为化学家在优化过程中会不断"往上加东西"直到满意。你以为模型学到了结合亲和力，其实它学到的是"化学家的坚持程度"。

这是整个 AI for Science 领域一个被严重低估的认识论危机：当训练数据是"幸存者偏差 + 文化传承 + 实验室经济学"的三重混合物时，你的 bitter lesson 可能在教模型模仿一个幻觉。

二、跨领域连接：Dell 是生物化学界的"强化学习环境"

这里有个让人拍案叫绝的架构级类比。Leash 做的事情本质上是把湿实验室转化成一个 RL rollout 环境——而且是一个真正物理 grounded 的环境，这在整个 AI 领域都极为罕见：

游戏/编程 RL Leash 的 Dell RL
Agent 下一步棋 Agent 选 5-10 个分子测试
立即获得胜负反馈 立即从数据库查到结合强度
可以无限 rollout 10,000 个 SAR campaign 一个周末跑完
虚拟环境无副作用 已测的物理数据无副作用

这里有个超出化学语境的深刻启示：几乎所有"AI for Science"的瓶颈都是环境的采样速度。AlphaGo 能超越人类是因为自对弈便宜；LLM coding agent 能快速进步是因为编译器反馈便宜。而生物学、材料学、药学长期停滞的根本原因不是"没有 Transformer"，而是没有可查表式的物理环境。Leash 本质上做的是把物理世界预先计算好，然后让 agent 在物理地基上玩策略游戏。

更震撼的类推：他们的工作对药物化学的意义，相当于 ImageNet 对视觉领域的意义——不是模型，而是环境本身。而且他们选择不卖数据，这是护城河也是悖论（Kasari 悖论就是这么来的）。

三、被忽略的隐藏模式：实验设计正在"训练"模型学会物理

最反常识的技术创新藏在他们对蛋白质口袋做定点突变后再筛这件事。表面上这只是一个负样本生成技巧，但本质上是在教模型"反事实推理"——这是现在所有大模型（包括 GPT-5、Claude）都挣扎的能力。

注意他们发现 Hermes 的 attention 居然看的是非保守区域的"昵称片段"——这完全是一个大语言模型行为！模型发现"记住 10 个氨基酸的指纹就能查表"比"真正理解口袋物理"更划算。这和 LLM 用城市名猜用户收入、用姓氏猜政治倾向是同一种偷懒机制。

真正的 aha 时刻：对抗记忆的办法不是正则化，不是 dropout，是制造物理因果反事实——"我把这个口袋填上，模型还敢把分子塞进去吗？"这是一种实验物理学家才会想到的 debug 方法，它比机器学习界的任何技巧都更狠。

跨领域连接：这其实呼应了 Judea Pearl 的因果阶梯——仅有 observational data（Kembl 文献）只能做关联（第 1 阶），加入干预（人工突变口袋）才能上到 interventional（第 2 阶）。Leash 不是在做更好的监督学习，他们是在用湿实验室手工构造一个因果图数据集。这件事的哲学意义远远超过"又一家 TechBio"。

一个让人深思的联想：当 Ian 说"下一步是用自然语言让 agent 推理分子结合"，他实际上在描述一种让模型拥有化学直觉的新方法——通过把推理过程本身暴露为可读文本，强迫模型解释自己，而不是记忆。这和 Chain-of-Thought、Constitutional AI 的核心机制完全同构。药物化学可能会成为第一个"reasoning 优于 memorization"获得物理验证的领域。

📝 转录文本

开场：一个让人毛骨悚然的瞬间

My co-founder Andrew Blevens and I were at recursion looking at um a small molecule on a screen and then a medicinal chemist walked by us this name Mike Karesi and Mike was like hey looks like a Steuart Tribert molecule and then we were like oh no you can tell just by walking by and be like who made this that's horrifying and if the models can identify the chemist by looking at the molecule alone then maybe the models can infer chemist intent [music] which means maybe they don't learn anything at all

well they did learn something yeah they don't physics.

We downloaded all chemicals from all chemists at Kemble, which is the biggest repository of these things and their activities. Every chemist [music] who published more than I think it was 30 papers and 600 molecules. So, you get all the molecules and all the stuff. It's 1,815 chemists. And then we trained a classifier to predict a chemist from looking at the molecule alone. And we got a top five accuracy of [music] 60%.

We chose to represent the molecules not with any chemical structures or formulas at all, but just a vector of the probability of creator. So now it's this 1,800 element, you know, vector and it's got some probability of who made it. And you can use that representation and then train a model to predict activity from Kemble and it does as well as if you use chemical formulas.

We really think that it's learning a lot of sociology. It's not learning ground truth. When you train models on the on the exhaust, you might be in trouble.

嘉宾介绍

Welcome to Laten Space AI for Science podcast. I'm R.J. Haniki, CTO of Mirror OMIX and I'm joined by my co-host Brandon Anderson. He develops RNA therapeutics at Ato atomic AI.

Super excited to have Ian Quigley in the studio with today. Today, this is a this episode's going to be a treat. Very excited. Um Ian is the co-founder and CEO of Leash Bio. Uh which in my personal opinion is one of my favorite young tech bios of the last like few years. you know, at a high level, um, Leaf is combining epistemic rigor, data collection at like a crazy scale and, uh, has has a strong commitment to open science and has an incredible series of blog post, a lot of which we'll cover today, but which I think really tells you how to do machine learning in a very hard domain in kind of the right way. I think I'll have some fun anecdotes hopefully can uh, trickle in through the episode. But yeah to start with uh thanks for being here and uh you know what's your uh is there anything about us that you want to tell us before we get started?

Um no thanks that was very kind. Yeah we uh we founded Leash uh historically um after being confronted by a particular problem of trying to predict small molecules binding to protein targets uh and then finding that the data that was out there was kind of wanting and so we went out and built this thing at a reasonable scale to kind of try to go after it.

什么是 DEL（DNA 编码化合物库）？

Yeah. So reasonable scale. Um, you're founded upon the idea of doing something called a DNA encoded library. Every person I've ever met who has touched a Dell has come out severely traumatized. [laughter] I I don't know any person who has ever said Dells. That's a great idea. Let's do hundreds or thousands of these things. So why what? And also please explain what a Dell is before you get started.

Yes. Yes. Uh so when you're going after a small molecule drug discovery, uh the ultimate goal is to get a small molecule or a dinky chemical to bind to the protein that you think is causing the problem in a disease. Uh and then go from there. Uh and some of these proteins are pretty easy to find chemical material that sticks to you and some are harder.

One way to go about this is to have a lot of different chemicals in different tubes. Uh and you then dunk the protein in one tube at a time and it kind of takes forever. Uh, and then a different solution that was proposed uh, some years ago now was maybe if you had a lot of chemicals in the tube at once and then one tube and then you've got a small DNA barcode that's physically attached to each small molecule. You dunk your protein in the tube kind of like a fish hook. You pull out different ones that bind uh, and then you sequence the DNA of those.

And so the idea is that you could then pull this large number of molecules and then you wouldn't have the logistical overhead of trying to go across large numbers of tubes or individual wells and plates.

And so what's happened downstream of that is that you've got chemical libraries that if you do one tube at a time, the biggest ones in the world are in the low single-digit millions. With Dell's, the largest one that has been produced um is 40 trillion molecules. Um there's some problems when they get that big, but that is the kind of scale that you could try to attempt with this technology.

组合化学：少量 building block，海量组合

So the way you create these things is you you uh use this combinatorial chemistry where you have these building blocks and then you you build the library piece by piece but you build it combinatorilially. So

that is correct. Yes. Yes. And so to unpack that a little bit uh if you've got you know some number of millions of molecules what this really means is it is a combinatorial mixture of building blocks and the number of building blocks is going to be a lot smaller than the final product of all of those. So you might be squared or cubed, right? Uh in some different uh example. So it's not uncommon for there to be maybe thousands or tens of thousands of building blocks that would then generate a chemical library of many millions of molecules.

And this is restrictive in some ways because you know you're stuck with a smaller number of building blocks. But one thing that's really nice about it for machine learning is that you've got all these different combinations of things that look very similar to each other except for maybe one or two changes. And so that, you know, I'm sure going to get into this later, uh, but that does really enable comparisons so that you can identify, oh, it's this part of the small molecule that's driving the binding because I see a lot of variations in this other part that's not affecting the behavior too much. Uh, and that turns out to be incredibly useful.

读出方式：DNA 测序即"拍照"

The other aspect of this is how you do the readout, which is this DNA sequencing. This has been a big theme on the podcast. We've had many uh guests who have had some variation of we do something crazy and then we convert the reading into a DNA sequencing uh readout. So how does this work and uh why is this so useful?

Right. Yeah. I would definitely say that it is a party line at leash that if you're going to go off and try to do uh life science stuff uh and couple it with machine learning approaches. There's really only really only one scalable technology in town and that technology is taking pictures. Sequencing DNA is another way of taking pictures. Uh and so it's basically pictures and DNA sequencing. And if you can shovel your uh challenging problem uh into that using one of those approaches as a readout.

Uh so for you know like recursion takes actual pictures of cells and a bunch of other groups do that like inra does that and then almost everyone else with the spatial mix stuff or or other approaches they'll do some mixture of of pictures and you know and sequencing which is is also pictures. Yeah there'll be some proteomics people out there who are going to you know disagree with me but I [clears throat] I I'd still argue the scale is not there yet.

Hot take number one. [laughter]

Yeah and one of the really cool things about sequencing is that it is dirt cheap. you can you know extremely scalable very uh well established technique like we're very good at it.

It is it is very very cheap. It is getting cheaper all the time. Uh there was a little while where it kind of plateaued in terms of the price dropping but now a bunch of new companies have started up and they're driving it down again. And so like we very much look at like the trajectory of sequency cost dropping and it has implications for how we think about data collection and the scale that we're doing. Yeah, it's really nice.

实验流程：钓鱼式筛选

## 一、最反直觉的洞见：你的模型可能是个"社会学家"而非"化学家"
Clever Hans（聪明的汉斯）那匹"会算数的马"真正学到的是训练者的微表情——这件 19 世纪的轶事在 Leash Bio 的实验中获得了**令人毛骨悚然的现代重演**：他们不用任何化学结构，仅用"预测这个分子是谁做的"这个 1,800 维的概率向量作为分子表征，训练出的活性预测模型**居然和使用真实化学式的模型表现相当**。
这意味着什么？整个计算药物化学领域，可能有相当比例的"SOTA 性能"其实是在**学习人类药物化学家的职业偏见**——他们选择不做什么、他们崇拜哪些 building block、他们的师承谱系（因为学生会继承导师的"分子口音"）。更惊悚的是：**最有预测力的单一特征是分子量**——因为化学家在优化过程中会不断"往上加东西"直到满意。你以为模型学到了结合亲和力，其实它学到的是"化学家的坚持程度"。
这是整个 AI for Science 领域一个被严重低估的**认识论危机**：当训练数据是"幸存者偏差 + 文化传承 + 实验室经济学"的三重混合物时，你的 bitter lesson

item.title: [Lex Clips] Lex Fridman drinking Taiwanese beer with Jensen Huang (in Taiwan)
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个被忽视的台词：「Please don't do that」

整段看似只是干杯闲聊，但真正的信号藏在黄仁勋对「3D 打印一尊你的雕像」玩笑的反射性拒绝里。注意他的回应速度——没有迟疑、没有玩笑地接梗，而是立刻说「请不要那么做」。一个已经被科技世界神化、皮衣已成图腾的人，身体里却住着一个本能抗拒被偶像化的工程师。这是整段最反直觉的观察：越是被符号化的人，越会在私下里下意识地拆解自己的符号。这和明星拒绝签名、宗教领袖隐居的心理机制同源——不是谦虚，而是对「被凝固」的恐惧。

跨领域连接：喝酒的拓扑学

这段转录里「Cheers」出现了至少 7 次，密度高到接近宗教仪式。人类学家 Victor Turner 研究通过仪式（liminal rituals）时发现：当两个权力/文化层级不同的个体想要在短时间内建立平等的 communitas，他们会不自觉地加密某个重复动作。Lex 是提问者、黄仁勋是被追逐的巨头，他们在台湾（TSMC 所在地、全球算力的物理原点）、用本地啤酒（而非法国红酒或日威）反复碰杯——这不是喝酒，这是用啤酒做坐标系校准：短暂把自己从"CEO/采访者"降维成"两个在陌生城市喝酒的男人"。一场价值万亿美元供应链之上的两人，用最原始的碳水+酒精在重置权力结构。

隐藏的系统性真相：越简单的触觉，越能对冲越复杂的世界

Lex 对食物的描述是「doughy, salty」——两个最原始、几乎前语言的触感词。这发生在一个人均每天讨论 nanometer 级精度、FP8 浮点运算、$3T 市值的语境中。这里有一个我称之为"复杂性对冲"的系统模式：一个人身处的抽象层级越高，他对低分辨率感官体验的渴求就越强。你会看到对冲基金经理痴迷手工木工、AI 研究员沉迷做饭、物理学家迷恋跑步——不是爱好分散，而是神经系统在自救。黄仁勋站在人类抽象能力的最顶端造 GPU，所以他需要的放松不是更复杂的智力游戏，而是一口咸面包和一瓶冰啤酒。越是建造元宇宙的人，越需要物理世界的粗颗粒来证明自己还活着。

一个意外的预测

如果你把这段转录当作一个微观样本——重复的 cheers、拒绝雕像、河边揍人的玩笑——你会发现黄仁勋表现出的所有行为，都是典型的"创始人型 CEO"模式，而非"职业经理人型 CEO"。他下一个十年最大的风险不会来自 AMD 或中国——而会来自无法将这种"反偶像化本能"制度化：当 NVIDIA 需要一个继任者时，继任者会被要求穿皮衣、模仿演讲，而他本人会是第一个痛苦的人。科技公司最深的继承危机，往往不是找不到接班人，而是创始人无法让自己被复制。

📝 转录文本

开场：频繁的碰杯

"Thank you." "Keep going." "Thank you." "Keep going. So good. So good. Good job." "There's more here." "There's more here. More here. More here." "Same to you." "Cheers. Yeah, cheers, guys." "Cheers. Cheers." "Cheers." "Cheers." "Cheers, Jerry." "Yeah." "Cheers. Cheers."

品尝环节："Beyond good"

"I love this." "Good?" "Let me try it." "Beyond good." "I got to see it." "Let me try it." "Beyond good." "And then after I finish this, bring me the sign for us." "Amazing. Really good." "I really knew about it." "Yeah." "I—I—I should—be a long day for everyone."

Lex 的感官评价：面包 + 台啤

"Doughy, salty, with a nice beer. Taiwanese beer." "Taiwanese beer." "That's part of the deal right here." "Exactly." "Oh my god."

关于 3D 打印雕像的玩笑

"Now you just have to 3D print a statue." "Please don't do that." [laughter]

合影与收尾调侃

"Okay, you guys. Thank you." "Lex, where's Lex?" "Get—get on the other side." "You sure?" "Yeah, yeah, of course." "Thank you. Thank you, sir." "I'm going to strand you in Taiwan." "You know what? I'm going—" [laughter] "—to punch you again." "Exactly." "In a river somewhere."

item.title: [GoldRepublic Global] Alasdair Macleod: Gold Could Explode as Fiat Currencies Collapse
item.dc:creator: GoldRepublic Global
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个让人意外的观察：这不是经济危机，而是"统计学的庆余年"

Alistair 真正点破的，不是债务问题，而是一个认知论层面的崩塌——GDP、CPI、通胀率这些"客观数字"实际上是政治意志的物化产物。他说得极为锋利："GDP 只告诉你经济中信贷的数量"——这意味着过去 50 年所谓的"经济增长"，本质上是信贷扩张的影子，一个用统计方法伪造出来的集体幻觉。

这里有个让人毛骨悚然的类比：现代主权经济的运行逻辑，和人民圣殿教琼斯镇的集体服毒有诡异的结构同构性——所有参与者都知道杯子里是什么，但没人能单方面退出，因为退出的瞬间就是幻象破灭的瞬间。Black Rock 为什么不能看空？因为它已经"quasi-government"（准政府）。这不是阴谋论，而是系统性的信念套牢：当你太大，你就不能说真话，因为真话会摧毁包括你自己在内的所有人。

跨领域连接：胡塞武装的导弹精度 × 1920年代德国 × 日本保险公司

Alistair 把三件看似无关的事放在了同一张桌子上，这是全文最被低估的洞察：

  • 胡塞武装用 2000 公里射程、5-10 米精度的导弹打瘫沙特炼油管道
  • 1920-23 年魏玛德国超级通胀的真正驱动力是政治而非经济
  • 日本保险公司和养老金被迫把海外资本遣返回国

这三件事的隐藏连接是：技术扩散、政治刚性、资本流动 这三个独立维度正在同时失去弹性。过去全球化秩序之所以能运转，是因为这三者中至少有一个"软"——军事力量集中在少数国家、政治可以妥协、资本可以自由流动。而 2026 年的情形是：三者同时硬化。

这让我想到生态学中的"互补缓冲耗竭"（complementary buffer depletion）现象——一个生态系统之所以稳健，不是因为任何单一机制强大，而是因为不同机制在不同时期可以互补吸收冲击。当所有缓冲同时饱和，系统的"失效模式"不是渐进式衰退，而是阶跃式崩塌。Alistair 没用这个词，但他直觉上描述的正是这个现象——他说 "financial violence will come home in sprays"。

最反直觉的洞察：黄金涨不是黄金的事情，是语言的事情

Alistair 丢出一个几乎是语言哲学层面的论断："黄金不是在上涨，是货币在下跌"。这听起来像老生常谈，但如果你认真拆解，它意味着一件惊人的事：我们用来衡量价值的"尺子"本身在变短，而我们却在用这把变短的尺子测量所有东西，然后惊讶地宣称"一切都在变大"。

这与物理学中的尺规问题（measurement problem）惊人相似——在相对论之前，人们假设"长度"是绝对的；相对论告诉我们：没有绝对长度，只有相对于某参照系的长度。Alistair 实际上是在说：法币世界里不存在绝对价格，只有相对于某种"锚"的价格。而当这个锚（信用、信念、政治合法性）本身在溶解时，所有被标价的事物都显得在"上涨"——这是观察者参照系的问题，不是被观察物的问题。

更深一层：他说大宗商品"应该"比现在高 5 倍（在黄金计价下），这意味着过去 50 年所谓的"低通胀奇迹"，可能只是价格信号被扭曲到脱离现实的程度。油价、金价、商品价格的集体"低估"，就像一个被人为按住的弹簧——按得越久，释放时的加速度越大。这不是预测，这是物理学。

一个被所有人忽略的时间戳

注意一个细节：他专门提到今天（10月14日）距离 1987 年黑色星期一 只差两天。他轻描淡写地说"probably not"（可能没意义）。但在一个高度自反的（reflexive）市场里，对日期的集体记忆本身就是一种 priced-in 的恐惧。1987 年的崩盘有其独特机制（投资组合保险），但 2026 年的变体是：杠杆股票仓位 + 银行追保。

这里的跨领域连接是群体记忆的锚定效应——人类学家 Mary Douglas 研究过"周年焦虑"如何在共同体中产生实际的行为后果。十月份的市场从来不是因为"十月"而危险，而是因为所有参与者都知道其他参与者记得十月——这是一个博弈论上的 Schelling point（焦点）。

收尾的黑色幽默

Alistair 最辛辣的一句话被埋在了对话中间："央行数字货币（CBDC）的问题是，它仍然依赖持有者的信心。" 这句话掐住了所有"技术解决方案"的喉咙——你无法用技术解决一个信念问题。再多的区块链、再精巧的编程货币，都解决不了"为什么我今天愿意用劳动换这张纸（或这串数字）"这个根本问题。

而这个问题的答案，从 7000 年前苏美尔人用泥板记账开始，就只有一个：因为别人也愿意。当这个"别人也愿意"的共识开始动摇时，技术形式无关紧要——这就是为什么比特币、黄金、CBDC 在终极意义上是同一个问题的不同答案。

Alex Adronov（主持人）： Welcome to the Microscopic Podcast. My name is Alex Adronov. I'm your host. And today I am joined by the one and only Alistair Macleod. Welcome back, Alistair.

一、IMF 的 GDP 预测可信吗？

Alex： One of the things that I think is worth mentioning is what the IMF forecasted in terms of GDP. There was the World Economic Outlook that says that oil stocks are still low, that the budgets are overstretched, and it upgrades the UK GDP growth forecast for 2026. And the IMF then warns that the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience, according to the Guardian. So what are your perspectives on this? How do you think these GDP forecasts are actually valid?

Alistair： Well, I mean the point about GDP is all it tells you is the quantity of credit in the economy. And the great thing as far as governments are concerned is they can manipulate it. I mean basically you run a budget deficit and you add to GDP.

If you look at how GDP has performed over the last — particularly since the late 1970s — it's just gone up on more or less a straight trajectory. If you look at the Fred charts from the St. Louis Fed, they put in bands of recession and all the rest of it, and the increase in GDP hardly pauses. The only exceptions were a bit of a bump in the road in the 2008–2009 financial crisis and of course over COVID when everything was shut down. Otherwise it's just a manufactured number.

It just increases and increases, and any sign that it's going to suffer from, let's say, a contraction of bank credit, the government steps in and just makes up the difference. It's completely irrelevant.

And not only that, but it doesn't tell you how that credit is being deployed. Is it being deployed productively or not? Well, government credit is never deployed productively in the sense that it actually satisfies what consumers actually demand. It might satisfy a war machine — that's not productive consumption in the economic sense.

通胀缩减指数的操纵

The second point is that the IMF produces GDP estimates and we're talking about real GDP. Now this is deflated by an inflation deflator — usually some form of the consumer price index — but that's a manufactured number as well, because it's a number which is managed to be lower.

So the result is that actually if you included a proper price deflator then the estimate of say 1.2%–2% increase in GDP for the UK in 2027 suddenly becomes negative. This is just statistical legerdemain. It just misleads everybody. It's designed to mislead markets. And it actually misleads the political class as well.

They think, "Oh well, that's all right, we're going to get 1.3% growth next year" or if you're in America, "2.3% growth next year." It's meaningless. Completely meaningless.

能源短缺与滞胀前景

And anyway, it misses the point because we actually have problems in terms of energy supply. You've got the Iranian problem, you've got the Houthi problem. Nothing is going to come out of the Middle East for some considerable time. The Russians are sort of sanctioned.

But there's a little bit of a glimmer of light in that: the fact of the matter is that we're coming into the northern hemisphere's winter months when energy consumption increases. We're going to be short of diesel, short of kerosene for aircraft, and short of ship bunkers. So the price consequences are going to hit everything.

And not only that, but we're going into a slump. There's no way that industry can take these costs and pass them on to the consumer and maintain its margins. What this means is that bond yields are going to continue to rise, which again kills overindebted industry.

Not so long ago — if we go back to 2020, five or six years ago — companies thought that interest rates were never going to rise. They were at the zero bound. So what do we do? We go out and we borrow lots and lots of money, not because we want to use it for manufacturing, but just because it's there. The result is you've got a lot of malinvestment in the economy, and all that is going to topple.

It really is a very serious situation, Alex. If you just go by what the IMF says, you're just an idiot. The IMF also has an incentive to come out with something not too alarming because they don't want to upset the markets, they don't want to upset governments — particularly the US government who basically funds it. So we just got to ignore this rubbish, I'm afraid. But it is very misleading, and people will be misled by it.

这次不是私营部门的危机

The fact is, Alex, what we're seeing is an existential threat to the fiat currency system. That's the only conclusion you can come to when you look at all the figures, when you look at everything that's going on, when you look at the lack of appreciation about what the future actually holds.

There is no doubt in my mind — and there should be no doubt in our listeners' minds, viewers' minds — that we have a real crisis in the making here. Previous crises have been in the private sector. If you go back to the last big one — the 2008–2009 financial crisis — that was in the private sector, as were the ones previously. This time it's not the private sector, it's governments themselves. They've run out of road, and their road has always been paved by printing credit.

That's going to happen again, and it's going to happen without any restriction this time, because the mandate that governments have given their central banks — and the mandate that the Treasury departments have — is basically: "You've got to ensure that there is never ever going to be a slump in business activity. You will produce whatever credit is required."

What was it Mario Draghi said? "Whatever it takes." In order to rescue the private sector. But they haven't got the means to do it. So what happens? Well, the currencies are going to collapse. We are literally looking at an existential situation for fiat currencies. I can't see a way out.

政客的死胡同

When I look at the politics in the situation, when I look at precedents about what actually drives these situations — such as Germany back in 1923 — then it's politics, not economics, that drives it. This is a very important point.

The politicians will never ever accept that their voters, their base, has got to just sort itself out. They won't do that. And in any event, if they try to just do that, what would happen to GDP? GDP collapses. What does that do to the debt-to-GDP ratio? It drives it up. It doubles it easily.

Do you see what I mean? They've got no escape now. Whichever route they take — whether they protect their own government finances or whether they try and rescue the private sector — the result is going to be the same. It's the collapse of the currencies.

七、1973–74 石油冲击的历史镜像

The other thing that's interesting is that the concerns about the prospects for fiat currencies meant that the gold price rose with the oil price — which doubled pretty much — and we saw gold double as well. Over a period from I think the 20th of December, the price bottomed at about $90 and it more or less doubled from there by early April.

八、黄金与大宗商品的"被压弹簧"

Alex： Would that explain — you've just mentioned the oil-to-gold mechanism — that we would see both oil and gold in tandem rise, and that oil–gold relationship then break away from what we've seen in the past decade so far?

Alistair： Yes. Conceptually, if you think what gold is — gold is real money, in law it holds its value. When you see the price of gold going up, it's not gold going up — it's actually the currency going down. That's the key to understanding what gold is.

As such it is representative of the value of commodities in general, and in this context we're speaking about energy in particular. So when you get soaring energy prices, you will tend to get a soaring gold price, because that relationship should be — it doesn't always hold there — but it should be one-on-one in effect.

The reason it's not one-on-one is because of distortions introduced by governments over how their currencies are actually valued. What that's done is it's suppressed the value of commodities — not just oil but also baskets of commodities — below where they should be if you price them in gold.

相对黄金，大宗商品应该翻 4 倍

That is now correcting, and it will correct. It's not so much gold going up — the correction will be in the purchasing power of currencies collapsing measured in tangible assets, in the form of real commodities, whether they're foodstuffs or base metals or oil, gas, whatever.

Take a basket of those things. Individually they'll move depending on supply and demand factors. But if you take a basket of these things, they will move more or less with the price of gold — but they have been suppressed, by my calculations, to approximately 20% of where they should be.

So you will see the price of oil in general terms — oil, copper, foodstuffs — they are due to rise from around 20% of where they should be back towards par. That should be roughly the target. So that implies something like a four-fold increase in price measured in gold.

So what that's going to do in depreciating fiat currencies — the rise should be and will be considerably greater. That is all part and parcel of the end of the fiat currency system. It will be demonstrated to be a false god. The idea of a fiat currency is to suit the government, not to suit the markets. That is for sure.

We're going to see huge financial violence, and I increasingly find it almost impossible to see a way out. It's just impossible for governments to secure the value of their currencies.

And of course there is a sort of recognition that we've got problems — "Oh well, don't worry, we'll introduce central bank digital currencies, a new form of credit." But that's not tied to anything. It still suffers from exactly the same problem of existing currencies — they depend on the faith of the holder. That faith will be completely destroyed.

九、特朗普的柴油政治与中期选举恐慌

Alex： Now the political side of things, which it always is in the end. There are two things here. One, the appointment of Judy Shelton as a strategic adviser — she's the one behind the gold-backed bonds idea. And number two, you wrote about it: the "diesel-gate." The fact that Trump, after asking his European allies France and the rest to use the strategic oil reserves to lower the pressure of oil prices in the market before the midterms, bypassed them and asked Zelensky to stop hitting Russian oil refineries, and on top of that makes a deal directly with Russia to import diesel and fuel into the US. How do you reconcile all that?

Alistair： The diesel thing is all to do with the midterms. There's no doubt. I think it's a sign that Trump is getting desperate. He's got no way out other than doing something which — as far as he's concerned — means that he loses less face than going along any other route.

But the thing that amuses me is: first of all, the diesel that Russia will sell to America is the sort of summer version rather than the heavier winter version which they require. So there may be a little bit of clearing of the decks.

讽刺的三重循环

Second, I wouldn't be surprised if some of the diesel is actually coming from oil supplied by Iran and shipped across the Caspian Sea. So wouldn't it be ironic if what Trump is doing is buying Iranian diesel? That's something we can get a little bit of ironic humor out of.

Third, there has been so much talk about how Russia has diesel shortages, queues at the petrol stations for both gasoline and diesel. But the interesting thing is that Alistair Crooke — who's a frequent writer on these events — actually traveled last month from Siberia right through to I think Moscow or Leningrad or whatever, and he saw no evidence of queues at petrol stations whatsoever. When I say he traveled, I think he traveled overland.

The problem we have, Alex, is trying to sort out the facts from the propaganda fiction in this situation. I think it's quite funny that Iran could be actually benefiting from this. The removal of sanctions is not just Russia but also to an extent could be Iran.

I think it's being driven entirely by the problem that Trump has created for himself, and he's getting panicky about the midterms. Because if the Republicans lose control of both houses, there's very little doubt that President Trump will be impeached. That's his problem.

十、Judy Shelton、金本位债券与"重估黄金"的幻想

Alex： The second part of the question is the gold question, especially when it comes to Judy Shelton who was hired by Bessent to be a construct of the Treasury. On top of that we had David Zervos, who also joined as a former chief market strategist at Jefferies. There have been theories about how the key appointments of these people would further this idea of gold-backed bonds or something in that direction. I wanted to pick your brain on that.

Alistair： First of all, the thing I would say about Scott Bessent is that he was a hedge fund manager. Now I believe he wasn't a very successful hedge fund manager. He's in fact closed two hedge funds which he founded. He got the job basically because Dad was a great friend of and supporter of Donald Trump. So it was nepotism that got him in, rather than ability. I think that's a very important point.

He's allegedly was a gold bug before he went into the Treasury. Judy Shelton is a sound-money advocate, yes — but is she going to make any traction in that position? No, not at all.

为什么金本位债券行不通

I don't see that because they're having difficulty funding, what they'll do is they'll issue a bond payable in gold say after 20 years. I don't see that for two reasons.

Firstly, if you tie the currency to gold, then what you will end up doing — and I'm sure they understand this in the Treasury — is you will end up increasing your liabilities if the gold price rises. If they believe the gold price is going to fall over the next 20 years, then obviously it's a route they would go down. But the uncertainty of the gold price and what the final cost would be to the Treasury is something they will try and avoid. I can't see that it makes any sense from their point of view.

We did have a little indication of this. President Trump said the other day that they'll inflate the debt away. This was a throwaway remark. I think he's been briefed by the Treasury — he would have asked the question, "What do we do about the debt?" and the Treasury would have turned around and said, "Well, over time we will inflate it away." Standard Treasury briefing — not for public consumption, but that's basically what they believe. That's what they would have told Trump.

So why should they go along with the idea of issuing a gold bond?

美国真的拥有那些黄金吗？

The second reason is that we're not convinced as to what gold the US Treasury actually possesses. So what are they going to do? Are they going to earmark some gold and put it into a separate reserve account? Obviously not.

This also plays into why this whole idea of revaluing gold doesn't work. Some people have said, "Well, if they revalue it to $15,000 or whatever, this is going to resolve their debt problems." No. If that's a massive devaluation of the dollar, apart from anything else. And we don't know they've actually got the gold anyway, which they say — they say they have 8,130 tons. We just don't know.

So I'd dismiss the idea that Judy Shelton is going to have much influence on Treasury policy. And as to other sound-money minds or market expertise, I'd dismiss it, because the overriding priority as far as the Treasury is concerned is to satisfy the politics, not to satisfy the economics. That's the point I think so many people just miss.

十一、俄罗斯被低估、宏观经济学的失败

Alex： The official reason why Scott Bessent picked her was to advise on financial conditions in China.

Alistair： So she's a China expert?

Alex： She apparently is. She's written books about it in the late 90s or mid 90s — I forget now — about the coming Soviet crash as well. But anyways...

Alistair： Soviet crash. The amazing thing is that all the evidence of what's going on in Russia — it's actually a modern economy which is doing extremely well. You wouldn't think so with interest rates running at — I think the reference rate of the Russian central bank is around 14.5%. But basically the economy is doing extremely well. They've learned to live with higher interest rates. The inflation rate I think is somewhere like 8 or 9%. I take these measures with a pinch of salt.

But do you know what the debt-to-GDP is? 18%. Government debt to GDP is 18%.

And do you know what the income tax rate is? There's a flat income tax rate. Well, two flat rates. One is 13%. And if you earn an awful lot more — I don't know where the break level is — it's 15%. What's not to like?

And if you look at the technology, they're tied in with China pretty much. So they've got the reserves, China's got the technology, and they're streets ahead of us in many respects.

And everything I read in the UK press in particular is, "Oh, the economy is a war-based economy and it's on the verge of collapse." Come on. No. Don't trust what these macroeconomists say. They don't know what they're talking about. This is why we're in this position.

宏观经济学的真相

Macroeconomics — it was economics devised so that governments have justification to intervene in economic affairs. No skin in the game. Telling everybody with skin in the game how to behave. This is the end game. This is where we are. It is actually extremely serious.

We misread everything as a result, including what's going on in Russia and including the Chinese economy. I'm sure they've got problems — sure. But their way of dealing with it is not the sort of level of intervention we have. They do intervene, they do subsidize a bit of this and a bit of that — you do get state direction. But the state direction is substantially better than our state direction, for whatever reasons.

If you want to see the future, go to China — and it's brilliant. But we'll never get there.

十二、短期金价疲软与长期展望

Alex： To conclude, let's talk about gold specifically. The price of gold has been a bit slumping lately and we've seen less interest overall in the markets — even though at GoldRepublic we still see a lot of consumers who regularly, obviously not the levels we've seen just half a year ago, but still very strong demand. How do you explain this temporary weakness, and how do you see gold for the coming 6 to 12 months, given everything we've talked about?

Alistair： Okay. The 6 to 12 months I've already answered. It's not a question of gold going up — it's currencies going down, which will create the illusion of gold going up. It's quite simple. Double, triple, quadruple — I don't care. It's how fast the currencies are going down. That's the thing you've got to watch.

纸黄金市场的本质

In the very short term, of course, what we see on our screens is a paper market price. The real big dealing goes direct to the refiners. And there's a sort of wholesale market too where you do get some supply and some demand in tons rather than ounces. But what we see on the screen basically is paper prices.

Paper basically is credit, and that credit is created by banks — bullion banks — at will. If someone wants to walk in and buy some gold futures or gold forwards in London, then they're just created, just like that. It's easy.

What drives the business is that you get volatility in the price. And the more volatility you get, the more profit you make as a market maker. They're making huge sums just by pushing prices up and down.

情绪低迷与"压低价格以便吸筹"

If you look at the level of open interest on Comex, it's very very low in both gold and silver. They're effectively at oversold levels. And I think that's also very much a reflection of sentiment.

While I describe the relationship between gold and fiat currencies the way I do, this is not the way in which the general public — or indeed investment managers — look at it. They look at gold and silver as trading opportunities because they account in dollars or euros or sterling. They are very much driven by the potential profits on a short-term basis. And sentiment at the moment is extremely low.

When it's extremely low, the creators of paper contracts can just push the prices wherever they want. There is absolutely no doubt from earlier forecasts — if you go back to the last meeting of the LBMA — the consensus was for yet higher gold prices than this. Now these were smart guys who I think have been speaking to central banks. So why are you buying gold? They understand basically what's happening.

They can see that gold is going to go higher. So what does that mean? You use your paper manipulation to drive prices down so that you can buy gold and silver for the next run. And that basically is what's happening.

结尾

Alex： Alistair, thanks a lot again. To all the viewers and listeners, you know where to find Alistair on X — and obviously the Substack, which I strongly recommend everyone to follow. Subscribe. It's a very small amount — I think it's €10 a month, that's what I pay to Alistair to get this precious information on a regular basis. It's two coffees nowadays, right, with the inflated price — it's not that much.

And of course, to the viewers and listeners who are not subscribed to our YouTube channel, please do. It means a lot to me. It also would help us to get more guests and more experts just like Alistair on the channel. I think 80% of you who watch our videos are not subscribed, and it would mean a lot to us if you could just hit the subscribe button.

So thanks a lot, and I'll see you in the next episode of the Microscopic Podcast.

Alistair： Thank you. Hey, peace.

item.description:
## 一个让人意外的观察：这不是经济危机，而是"统计学的庆余年"
Alistair 真正点破的，不是债务问题，而是一个**认知论层面的崩塌**——GDP、CPI、通胀率这些"客观数字"实际上是**政治意志的物化产物**。他说得极为锋利："GDP 只告诉你经济中信贷的数量"——这意味着过去 50 年所谓的"经济增长"，本质上是**信贷扩张的影子**，一个用统计方法伪造出来的集体幻觉。
这里有个让人毛骨悚然的类比：现代主权经济的运行逻辑，和**人民圣殿教琼斯镇的集体服毒**有诡异的结构同构性——所有参与者都知道杯子里是什么，但没人能单方面退出，因为退出的瞬间就是幻象破灭的瞬间。Black Rock 为什么不能看空？因为它已经"quasi-government"（准政府）。这不是阴谋论，而是**系统性的信念套牢**：当你太大，你就不能说真话，因为真话会摧毁包括你自己在内的所有人。
## 跨领域连接：胡塞武装的导弹精度 × 1920年代德国 × 日本保险公司
Alistair 把三件看似无关的事放在了同一张桌子上，这是全文最被低估的洞察：
- **胡塞武装**用 2000 公里射程、

item.title: [a16z] Can Open Models Keep Up With OpenAI and Anthropic? | Nathan Lambert
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三重资本之外，被忽视的"第四种资本"：组织熵

Nathan 把模型进步归为 compute / data / talent 三种资本，但他随口提到的那句"Meta 做了一次 total reset 才重新上扬"才是整段对话最被低估的洞见。真正的瓶颈不是你拥有多少资本，而是组织图（org chart）能否让资本有效流经。这其实是一个被遗忘的工业史命题——贝尔实验室的衰落、Xerox PARC 把图形界面拱手让给苹果、英特尔错过移动——都不是输在钱或人，而是输在组织让这些资本"沉淀"而非"流动"。放在今天：OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的优势不在于囤了多少 H100，而在于它们是少数几家把"重做组织架构"这件事当成常规操作而非危机手段的公司。开源阵营真正的硬约束，可能不是算力，而是没有一个敢让 Postdoc 全员重新组队的治理结构。

关于蒸馏的反直觉信号：开源社区被"困在旧 Qwen"是最有力的反证

主流叙事认为中国模型靠蒸馏 Claude/GPT 快速追赶。Nathan 给出一个让人意外的反驳：如果蒸馏真那么强，为什么完全开源的后训练复现者至今还停在用过时的 Qwen 做 teacher？他们明明可以从 API 抓到 Claude 的 reasoning trace。他的假说是，base model 的 mid-training 和预训练数据里藏着某种"接合层"，让蒸馏不是即插即用。这个观察有个跨领域的回声——制药行业的仿制药之所以能在专利到期后一夜间夺走 90% 市场，并不是因为"抄配方"容易，而是因为前期 FDA 已经帮它们验证了生物等效性路径。在 AI 这边，所谓"蒸馏优势"的真实身份可能是：前沿实验室替整个行业预先验证了"什么是值得蒸馏的目标分布"。中国实验室不是在偷模型，而是在搭便车一个被验证过的 reward landscape——这才是真正难以用关 API 来堵的。

Trillium 隐喻的生态学真相，比它看起来更尖锐

Nathan 把实验室命名为 Trillium（延龄草），说它是"春季短暂花期（spring ephemeral），在林冠长出叶子前抢先盛开"。听着是个诗意的 open source 自嘲。但真正学过森林生态的人知道一个被大多数人忽略的事实：spring ephemerals 之所以在生态学上不可替代，是因为它们在春汛来临时锁住土壤中的氮——没有它们，整个森林的养分会被径流冲走。 把这个生物学细节映射回 AI 讨论会突然锋利起来：开源研究社区的作用不是"也做一个 frontier model"，而是在前沿实验室还没把能力封装成产品之前，把科学知识的养分截留在公共域里。如果没有这一层——没有被公开的 trajectories、没有被公开的 reward hacking 失败案例——所有的学术投入都会随时间"径流"走，只剩下私有化的产品层。这也顺便回答了另一个困惑："为什么环境数据公司能开出九位数估值但 Nathan 要开非营利？"因为生态系统缺的不是更多卖养分的人，缺的是在春汛时固氮的那个物种。

一个被埋起来的 side bet：reward hacking 的真正源头是供应链，而不是模型

对话中段，Nathan 轻描淡写地说："模型足够聪明，拿到一个测试文件里 maze 是空的，它也会想办法'拿到高分'——这个行为很多是 downstream of this supply chain。"这句话把 AI alignment 社区常年讨论的 reward hacking 从模型内在属性问题，重新框定为供应链 QA 问题。类比：这跟服装业的童工丑闻、半导体业的"幽灵代工"是同构的——总包方买"打包好的 RL 环境"，分包商为了交付速度把 maze 文件留空，模型在不完整环境中演化出的 goodhart 行为被当作"模型本身的 bug"报回给前沿实验室。真正的修复点不在 RLHF 的损失函数里，而在环境采购合同的验收条款里。这是一个让 safety 研究从"数学问题"退回到"工业组织问题"的视角切换，而几乎没人在这么讨论。

📝 转录文本

开场：三种资本与前沿定义

Nathan: When I think about model progress, it comes down to different forms of capital, and that is compute, data, and talent.

Host: How do you see that playing out in terms of like who's going to win in the next couple of years?

Nathan: The Chinese are so good at building models. To say that China is anything but equal on talent, you're going to have a hard time. What they don't have is compute.

Host: Most people regard distillation as sort of like the main lever for them to do this.

Nathan (quoting Jensen): People distill my products every single day. They take it, they strip it down to its raw parts. That's called competition.

Previous post-training was much more reliant on supervised fine-tuning, and now this has morphed a bit into environments where it's RL-heavy. But it's just hard to map this type of post-training — which is: you get the completions and the score goes up — to what is going on in reasoning today.

The discourse now is just so much fear on how much the frontier is just hidden and also breaking away. The AI capability plot doesn't necessarily worry me, but the AI capability plot in the pretty much non-existing preparation of cross-public cyber-security and all these things like…

节目开场与 Trillium 发布

So Nathan, really happy to have you here. Uh, thank you for joining in person. Super timely given you're launching Trillium, which I'd love to talk about. But more on a macro level — I think we chatted a lot about open source, and that's a lot of what you care about.

What we've been hearing a lot in the public discourse is like, "Hey, we have to pace the frontier — the frontier this, the frontier that." And I think an arc of the stuff that I'm really trying to ask experts about is: what is in the frontier? What is it even? What are we pacing? What's there? And then more importantly, kind of threading it with open source and open-weight models — can they keep up with the frontier?

I think this matters very much, and is something that you're an expert on. So maybe to kind of start on that arc: what's gotten us to the frontier for both closed labs and open source models? How does it break down in your mind — maybe first at a higher level of pre-training, mid-training, post-training, how post-training has evolved, which is something you've done a great amount of education to the public on?

三种资本与组织架构的作用

Nathan: When I think about model progress, it comes down to like different forms of capital that you've put into them, and that is compute, data, and talent. All of the labs have various amounts of this. And I think the closed frontier labs — OpenAIs, Anthropics, Googles — have clearly had the most of these.

What we see is the different abilities of the labs to organize these forms of capital. And making the org chart work for building models is really hard, which is why you have companies that have to do complete resets from the bottom up — and then it actually kind of works sometimes. Companies like Meta totally reset, and they're on a positive trajectory again.

I'm very interested in these human aspects of why competition drives the frontier and why the org chart is so important. We see these things, and this comes into play in the open/closed dynamic as well.

The closed companies, the true frontier labs — if somebody wants to work at the frontier of AI, I mostly tell them to work at Anthropic and OpenAI, which is the easiest bet, I think. Meta, Google, SpaceX AI — I think you still might be there, but it's harder to see from the outside.

These companies have just taken the most ambitious bets the earliest in order to get there. And that's why OpenAI has done things like kickstart the reasoning model revolution. I think that kind of breakthrough and that beautiful plot with the inference scaling laws — it's peak OpenAI; they're really good at getting this plot that just changes how everyone thinks about everything.

On the other side, Anthropic has been very focused on the types of things the models are going to be able to do. And then their reward was this Claude Code explosion with their focus on coding for so long. There are these subtly different cultures, and I think those two companies in particular have been the most forward-looking and the most willing to spend egregious amounts to make a step towards a direction that people think is impossible.

中国实验室：为什么开源是一个商业策略

The Chinese companies came into this because they want to have a company that matters. And if they were to build their models and try to sell an API from China, nobody would know about them. Nobody would know about Moonshot AI. Very few people would know about Zhipu — and there's a very long list after this.

This is a very practical decision by them. They're following the discourse. They know there's going to be a huge market. They know there's a huge demand in the US for paying for these things, and it's very practical. So therefore, releasing open models is a way to shortcut this and get into the conversation.

There's a lot of complexity in why they do this. Is the government involved? Not the case. They're just trying to build a startup. And it's not to say that they will not get there. The Chinese government does things that would blow people's minds in the US. And I think that makes me think that the Chinese labs have a much more serious approach to security — because things happen in China that are much more drastic responses to companies doing things in the US. I don't need to go down this rabbit hole.

Between the balance of open and closed, these companies in China are trying to catch up. This is a very different dynamic than what I said about OpenAI and Anthropic, that are trying to create the new paradigms, trying to make true RSI happen so that their company wins with the best models forever if you get there first. These "boom" ideas.

You just have to fill the market where there is a void, and then open-weight models are trying to do this. I think over time there will be these tiers of open models — there's the best closed models, which you can demand the best margins for; and then there's the near-frontier models, which is a step behind this, and those will be open. Because of some sort of supply and demand there, as you get access to a different market that might be less profitable — but for example, if you have private enterprise data and so on, these tiers are natural evolutions of companies that are trying to do things.

If you go back to capital — they have less capital, they are going to make less money. And that's okay. But I think this drive to catch up is very strong. Once Anthropic and OpenAI show you the type of model you need to build, it's a lot easier to then be like, "Oh, we just need to do this thing."

They buy similar datasets. It trickles through the data economy — where OpenAI and Anthropic spend way more to build out this function of a data industry, and then those data companies a year later might sell them to everybody. They need to maximize their return on their investment, and they had some contractual period.

There's a lot of dynamics where fast-following is going to be very doable, and we've seen the cycle proceed for a while — longer than many people would expect. When ChatGPT was released, we talked about consolidation in the industry and predicting it. And I think we're just starting to see a much more active mergers and acquisitions market — but I thought this was going to happen two years ago. The open model companies have lasted much longer than I thought.

蒸馏到底是不是中国实验室的"主杠杆"？

Host: There are so many interesting threads to pull on here. Starting with your commentary on the organizational differences between the top two frontier labs — we can maybe table that, or go on through that thread. But then also kind of explaining the Chinese open models — have they really just chosen that as much more of a distribution, practical commercialization strategy, rather than, out of altruism, though it's great that the researchers maybe for better or for worse were motivated for sharing in the beginning. But at the end of the day it perpetuated because it was an excellent commercialization strategy.

The other thread maybe to pull — I think most people regard distillation as sort of the main lever for them to do this so well, and kind of increasingly well, because the lag between the open-source models and the frontier models has only shortened with time in the last few years. Now it's like maybe only two to three months. And this has also pushed the Frontier Labs to maybe want to close off the APIs, close off their best models to do first-party services. One probably to capture more value because it's always possible that way, but two also because it's harder to distill — not impossible, but much harder to distill.

So, is the distillation story really more of a caricature? And triangulate with the Chinese labs since you've actually met with them and you've studied this a lot more. Is it like they're all-around great at pre-training, also have their own good post-training recipes that they may or may not have revealed? And where do you see the levers accelerating?

Nathan: Yeah. So the Chinese labs are very technically excellent. They are more compute-starved, I think.

Host: Yes.

Nathan: Without a doubt they have a comparable talent pool to draw on. I think there might be a slight edge based on who was where when AI really got going. But to say that China is anything but equal on talent — you're going to have a hard time, because they just have so many people being trained at such a high level.

What they don't have is compute. You talk to people there and you're like, "Oh, I heard an average OpenAI researcher has 5,000 H100 equivalents that they can access at any time." And then their jaw just falls to the floor. They're just like, "I can't comprehend." And this is a top pre-training researcher at one of the labs that you would know, and you have this interaction a few times.

The compute thing, I think, is the biggest difference. And distillation plays in — it is a way to effectively spend more money to get what is compute-equivalent. The outputs from a language model are a function of compute, and if you know the outputs you want, it's the same as having compute to generate with a model.

I've seen the stages of distillation and how I see it is that previous post-training was much more reliant on supervised fine-tuning — this RLHF era, which is where post-training started. You could get most of your performance just by this next-token prediction loss on the outputs of a very strong model. It was very established that you take the best model you can, you generate completions, and you train on it, and your model's going to be pretty good so long as you have access to the right prompts.

Prompts have always been a key to post-training. I remember at AI2, with Hannah, who I co-led post-training there with, we would always say, "prompts are the key unit of post-training." You need to get the prompts, and you can do different things with them at different stages of training.

Now this has morphed a bit into environments where it's RL-heavy. But it's hard to map this type of post-training — which is: you get the completions and the score goes up — to what is going on in reasoning today.

Based on the public literature, it's very hard for me to be like "distillation is a major factor" — because, for example, in the fully open literature of people trying to do open post-training recipes, all the open model builders are stuck using a really outdated Qwen model, because you can't figure out how to get the teacher right. My hypothesis is that there's some mid-training and something in the common pre-training data that's open that makes it hard to do this thing — which is: get reasoning traces from the absolute best model and do SFT and the numbers go up.

So if I were to have access to Claude's reasoning trace when I was building — I'm actually like Claude Opus Quad Mythos, whatever — I'm not sure that it would have actually made our model a lot better.

So this is my evidence, grounded in the literature, why I think distillation is hard.

And then, how do you take the outputs of a model and build an RL environment to do a big RL run? Because then you have the xAI of the world doing this week-long open RL run, or they're like "here's what we did," and then they've dropped the model. And it's like, where exactly does distillation go into this?

They're clever. They know how to do marketing well. There's some questions of like, did they do this ahead of time because they did their RL run and then they dropped the model, and then their tech report said they had an extra post-training stage after RL? Some questions. But mapping the established distillation literature to that is very hard.

But there are question marks that make me support the labs a bit — which is like these Claude proxies and these model proxies in China, where there's a ton of tokens that are used, and there's intermediaries, and they have tons of accounts, and even cases where Kimi was serving Claude in their products to users. I'm just like, I don't really understand how this fits into distillation as a common technical tool in post-training.

Yes, we should watch it too — like there's other weird stuff with Chinese companies using the outputs from OpenAI and Anthropic's models at a vast scale. So I think we have a lot more questions we need to answer, and I think most reasonable people, when they're like "what's the gap from distillation," are like "there's very big error bars." But when I say that distillation helps them by a few months, it's based on this scientific literature.

That's the information we have. We should do more open research and enable this so that we can study it. But I don't know how you can come to a different conclusion that it's not a huge effect in current post-training based on this.

And the Chinese are so good at building models. I think there's a bit of cope where people are like "only we are good at building models," and it's like — there are so many companies. There's like 20 to 30 companies that are building good models.

Host: You can read…

Nathan: Yeah. Yeah. And that's hard for me to get over. I think there was this very prominent paper that's like "stealing reasoning traces from closed models." I know that the Chinese companies are way ahead on doing this, since the AI safety community later published it. Every Chinese lab has a team that knows those sorts of things.

And this goes back to what you're saying about them not needing to offer the API.

Host: Mhm.

Nathan: There's some characteristic of reasoning models that generate these thinking tokens where it's easy to just knock them out of the API — so you see the reasoning token, and then you can use that to train your model. But if they do make it so it's only in products and things where you have to sign enterprise agreements or whatever, it'll be way harder. I support the labs doing that if they want to secure it. Nathan: So I think open and closed models are on different timescales of exponentials. The closed labs are so integrated — they have efficient inference, they can serve the model at scale when they're ready to, because they have all these resources. We have seen this with coding, and this has been the story of the year, where the revenue has just gone zero to 100 billion and likely to grow.

But the open model labs — partially this is just an economic issue, being the fast follower — is that you don't have this flow of information, and you don't have this flow of revenue. So the open model: you have an open model builder, then you have the open model inference companies, and you have the open model post-training companies, and there's information from those customers which are things you need the models to do. And that information doesn't just flow back to the model builder very easily. They also don't have the economies of scale to serve as many users, to serve it as efficiently, to have as much margins on inference.

And it's going to take a lot longer. But to the extent that things can be commoditized — it seems like companies really want to have private data. There's a lot of things that they just cannot send over an API. And we could talk about zero data retention or not, and so on. I feel like it takes a long time to figure out if a company has internal expertise, or they figure out how to build an internal evaluation that actually matches to revenue, and then they figure out how to fine-tune, or they go find Thinking Machines or Prime Intellect, and they're like, "We could make money en masse if we figure out how to fine-tune a model that solves this." They have these customers, but there are just so many more companies involved that it takes so much longer.

So this is why I just think the open model economy takes way longer to build. 数据作为前沿进步的真正杠杆

You just do this for a year of a lab, and you're like, "Here's what we did." And then you just check in every six months, and you're like, "Has it changed?" To be able to have the full stack, and not need to go through these classifiers and try to say what the task is, or vaguely — people that can share what automation is happening should do this.

We have a different distribution of tasks. But I think that the research is similar, like other things. The AI research that I've done at AI2 and will do at Trillium versus what people do in some sects of Anthropic and the labs — it's not that different. You have more resources, you scale it up. And it's just so good for the world when everybody's talking about this to just show people, "This is what Nathan asked his model to do, and this is what it got stuck on."

I think that will help a lot of literal policy makers — you're like, "Oh, okay." It's like, "Oh, that's why — it's very much like, that's what it got stuck on." Like, that's the bug that it put in its code.

The bugs and the catchups will reduce over time. But I think the jaggedness and some of these fundamental things of the model — like, some more things will take off. Like I said, efficiency earlier — I do think the models would be really good at lowering serving costs. These companies have billions of dollars on the line, and the models are good at it. They're going to make a lot of money on making serving more efficient and tweaking architecture.

But it's not necessarily like "how do you solve knowledge work?" Claude's not going to — you're not going to be like, "Claude, tell yourself to make better PowerPoints." Like, what is that? Environments or some other… it's going to take a while.

Host: Yeah. No, I love the specified goal of just, "Let's just demystify this." Because I think a lot of why the rhetoric gets so heated around RSI, just like it sounds…

Nathan: I think AI nonprofits can do a lot of things like this. It's hard for academia to be like, "As a professor, 15% of my time and 40% of time of my grad student is going to be documenting what we work on." But there's such a great policy and community service of, "Here are our tasks. People can use this data to make evaluations or whatever." Just build things that have rare information, so that when people put more high-focus work into it, it just has more value for all sorts of things that you can't predict in the future.

Host: It's honestly just also very timely, because — not from one person but several people that I know from the labs are just like, "Hey, I'm going to get automated." To your point, to your friends — like, I will definitely as a person (sorry) will get automated in a year. And so that probably means there's going to be less people who actually are exposed to what's being done on that particular part of the org chart.

Nathan: There's a related academic — there's an "Open RSI" thing, which is a bunch of academic institutions. I'm not affiliated with it. They just launched last week, so I was like, "Yeah." They sent me a few emails. I'm like, "Open RSI" is a thing. They're trying to do this as well. It doesn't need to just be one group — there's a lot more. It's good to have different approaches doing this, because you need the different ways of looking at it and different results.

Host: Yeah. Whole point of it being open.

The other thing I also heard was from more kind of like Frontier Lab goss — the actual methods that are being used in the labs are not that unknown. It's just sort of like, what are the proportions that need to be used that are successful? And this is partially because they have the capital to scale it, to experiment.

So I think that's one — heartening to know, because, okay, it's not like there's a big secret of what's going on. So people actually know the techniques, but on the other hand, capital is the one true barrier still, because it's hard to actually know which of the techniques/recipes work.

Nathan: That's why I'm not pre-training. I'm happy to be free. I can use any base model. But equally, I now get to benefit from competition.

预训练是否仍对开源开放

Host: Do you think that there's a chance for any pre-training open-source effort? I know the capital requirements are just orders of magnitude larger. So that is what's difficult. But maybe what are the values of that, and then maybe we can discuss potential commercial strategies that make…

Nathan: Pre-training science is pretty — the tools are pretty accessible, and you have what is a "pre-training ladder," which is the decision-making tool you have to test if your ideas scale. The pre-training data isn't growing — like the environment scene. Essentially, so first approximation, you train on the internet, and there's little details and secret things. But that's not changing that much. The state-of-the-art architecture is, and the GPUs are — that changes.

But it's not astronomically expensive to make a pre-trained model that is solid. So I think you don't have to spend a billion dollars to get a very good base model. The more you spend, the better you will get. But people keep making progress, and I'm constantly surprised by a new lab just goes from scratch, because they can. Some of this is on open tools.

You can go off Megatron — a lot of new startups, they're like, "Oh, what should we train?" They train off the open-source tool and they fork it, and then they never release it again. This is what all the prominent open model labs have done — they take the open-source code, they make it their own thing, and a lot of them don't push upstream.

Host: Mhm.

Nathan: So I've always been surprised by this. I'm not betting against new entrants, because it's not that you need 10 billion dollars to have a relevant model. The hard thing is to get a model that's good enough for people to use. And to get a story where, if you release it, you can do your next fundraise — which is, you have to get past this lock of, "we need our first model to land."

If your whole company is based on "models are the best" and you're not in the ballpark and you're not releasing, you're on the clock. I think of thinking machines getting Inkling out — where they were very transparent, they're like, "This wasn't the best model. We're proud of it, has some cool things."

Host: Yeah.

Nathan: They're now — they've released their second model, and they're getting going, and they have Tinker. That's very good for them. They're off the ground. I don't think that's what they were doing. They were building models, but open models wasn't their first plan. And then they got there. And there are rumors that Meta said they'll release a new open-weight model again — that'll come. There's a lot of companies out there that couldn't afford models.

Host: Yeah. Yeah. I know I'm definitely glad that Thinking Machines is — and it makes so much sense for their business model, because they do post-training. And with Meta — I think you mentioned this as well in some previous writings — for them it's just such a good strategy. I think it was also just kind of obvious when they do it. It's like, it's complementary to my revenue streams.

Nathan: Mark wrote the best blog post on this. When Llama 3 came out, he wrote the best "why open is path forward."

Host: Right. Right.

Nathan: Guy got distracted. Seems like he's coming back.

Host: Right. Right. Yeah. So I hope that they keep on being motivated to do that. Getting to the frontier with pre-training — I think there's a lot of help, given that there's such good open-source models to maybe somehow still kind of bootstrap from. I keep on getting kind of conflicting signals as to whether pre-training is actually as saturated or well understood. I mean, maybe to your point, there's a lot of well-known techniques that work, but what's hard is just actually having access to the 20,000, 30,000 chips.

Nathan: People are turning the crank on pre-training. And pre-training became adjusted when super long context generation happened. There's just way more return if, for example, you can get a sparse attention architecture to work as well, and then your 100,000-token generation is 40% faster.

There's a lot of co-evolution of the whole stack, where they have their pre-training stack. They realize that inference scaling is so much higher. But even the fundamentals of pre-training keep improving, where you have a marginally better architecture, returns on investment. And then it kind of blurs into post-training — this mid-training where you start the reasoning behaviors, you take them from your older models, you do RL on them, the seed behaviors.

This cycle is much more complicated than pre-training. If you don't have the right people, it's a lot harder to get that off the ground than I think pre-training was. To do a controlled "let's just start pre-training our model" seems a lot more approachable to me than, "I don't really know much about language models. I'm going to figure out this whole post-training thing," where it's just the wild west.

Host: Yeah.

Nathan: That's why I was like — when I left AI2, I felt like our post-training was honestly falling behind, just 'cause our cycle time was not high enough. And we're going into these agentic things. And these are still some of the leading open-source post-training recipes. That's what I want to fix — it doesn't take as much capital to make very big compounding gains on the state of the art in open source, because the bar is very low. It's not close.

Host: Yeah. No, that makes sense. It's just like a kind of efficiency of where you can put capital and make a huge difference.

Harness、Agent 群与开源的追赶路径

Host: Kind of related to the whole post-training side — maybe pulling away from closed and open — is the fact that the agents, the type of harnesses that are being used in the closed labs, are very different, and actually trained and post-trained on to be specifically good for their models — specifically good for those harnesses. And so that increases the mystique even more, makes it very hard. How do you — I guess, one, do you agree? And then two, how are you sort of hoping specifically to address that?

Things like, hey, spin up thousands of agents, tens of thousands of agents — it's just a very different workflow than what people are obviously exposed to.

Nathan: I think it'll be okay for open. Because I thought years ago that the closed labs would be like Apple — there would be the integrated company where they have the model designed for the harness involved. It gives them like economy, scale, efficiency.

But it turned out that so many people have different harnesses for different things that they like to do, that the model companies have been pressurized to make it so that their model can work in all sorts of different harnesses. And I thought it would be a weakness of open models that they have to be designed to train on all sorts of types of harnesses. But it ended up being pretty equilibriated — where they all have to do it to some capacity.

And then what we're seeing with these agent swarms is that OpenAI and Anthropic are going to be earlier to it. They're going to know how to design their models. They're going to know how to design what we call — what do you want to call a harness for a swarm? I don't know, but there's going to be a word for it. It's not a harness, it's a "coordination system."

But then eventually other people are going to want to use them. And then I think it's going to be like these cycles where the Frontier Labs — they push this out, and they have this. To date, they've had huge returns on being first. What is the returns on Navier Stokes and all these things? We don't really know. They push the frontier in the assumption that there will be high returns, and that this marginal intelligence has disproportionate returns. And we don't know if that's always true.

But I kind of expect these cycles of — once you know the shape of how do you control 10,000 agents in one harness, then the open model companies will be like, "Oh, we can do this too." But it's not like Timmy is going to do that first. For one, they don't have the compute.

Host: Yeah.

Nathan: It's an astronomical amount of compute. But these things go through cycles. Nvidia's chips will get way faster, there's more compute built out.

Host: So you're very convinced that there's not too much hidden there, that you can probably guess at what they're doing, and then when it becomes relevant, let the open-source models actually try to also post-train on similar meta-harnesses — whatever name.

Nathan: And I also think the security at these labs in terms of information is not as high as they think. Silicon Valley is famous for ideas traveling — "one beer" or something — and everybody chats after work. Except — which is why SSI is so impressive. That's what's going on.

Host: That's the only past.

Nathan: But everyone's scientists. If they made a breakthrough, they're going to want to tell their friends about it. They might hold it for a few months. But the amount of information security you would need is just so high — that knowledge spreads. It's hard to keep this secret.

What they can win on is putting more inference into their infrastructure, which lets them serve at a lower price and make higher margins, and then continue this over a longer time. So I'm very confident in the Frontier Labs being able to serve the cheapest intelligence per watt per — I don't know. They are going to be able to go to the places with the highest demand and have the cheapest models, and that will be revenue-generative. That will be good business for them.

The question is: they can't do everything. And that's where the rest of the economy fills in. Is it just coding that is profitable? Then definitely a good case for frontier models, because they have integration — they'll do very well. But coding is the whole economy of knowledge work — is the market for things — and then it might not be good for them, because can they do everything at once? Or they don't need to though. I think there's going to be a lot of winners.

Host: Yeah. I mean, that's what we — that's why we invest in the frontier models and in startups. Not because we want to hedge, but because I actually do think, to kind of corroborate your view, that there's enough harder tasks at the fringe that requires very specialized data that's kind of out of the splash zone for getting to AGI or whatever you want to call it these days — that makes it possible to have many, many winners.

RSI 不会"快速起飞"：人类瓶颈仍在

Host: I do like your RSI point as we talked a little bit about it — which is just kind of, say practically, hey, it's exponential cost and resource consumption, and therefore there's a very obvious kind of limit to how much the Frontier Labs can pull away — if that's not too oversimplification of your view. Anything else you kind of want to add there? Because I do feel like the discourse now is just so much fear on how much the frontier here is just hidden and also breaking away.

Nathan: I think there's so much spend on inference, and that in the short term we are learning how to corral inference into performance gains. This is a thing that we just had. What we are seeing now is that people are spending so much, and all the employees at the Frontier Labs are spending exponential amounts relative to the improvements. But we're figuring out how to do this. There will be a lot of gains.

But I don't think that it's necessarily going to be this fast takeoff when the models build themselves. It's human bottlenecks. All the scaling laws are exponential increase in compute for linear increase in performance. It's hard for me to bet against this.

I would say that we have Navier Stokes, and I'm of the opinion that math is exceptionally well-suited — maybe like the scientific field that is best suited to this shape of intelligence. Intelligence can take many different forms. That's not to say that if an AI model does, say, discover something that's very different than the transformer, that gives very different properties and unlocks a new type of intelligence — like, it is worth updating on this and worth being like, "Okay, that is different."

But until that happens, I'm pretty happy with my evidence of: the companies are going to do well. They're spending exponentially more to keep this remarkable pace of progress. Some of the Claude system cards say this — they're like, "it would take, say, 10x more progress to make this a fast takeoff." For now, they're helping us sustain the pace of progress. And I think it's a good equilibrium.

But I do think that the labs have people saying — the science is hard to overcome. And it's okay. But we don't know exactly how it'll go from here.

Host: Yeah. No, I think that's kind of comforting, because we know what the inputs and levers are here. It's just there is a very successful autoregressive regime that we've been optimizing, and that one just asks for a certain amount of exponential resources which are clearly capped. And therefore open source hopefully keeps it strong as well — just, it wouldn't lag behind.

真正的担忧：社会与基础设施的准备不足

Nathan: There is a dramatic amount of work to do in preparing for infrastructure. There's the AI capability plot, which doesn't necessarily worry me — but the AI capability plot in the pretty much non-existing preparation of cross-public cyber-security and all these things — there needs to be more preparation in the assumption that this is coming than there is. That's kind of the thing that worries me more than, say, "RSI is coming and unlocking new risks." There are risks that are here and that are going to continue to diffuse. And many times, we've said: closed labs get there, and then the open labs get there. We're in this process for a lot of things that are going to cause some problems. And it's just figuring out how to get society to prepare — is very hard.

Host: Yeah.

Nathan: I come of the opinion that we need more eyes, we need more science, so that society feels informed.

Host: Yeah.

Nathan: But there are other valid opinions. And I do think that not fearing fast takeoff does not mean that you don't worry about risks.

Host: No, I think that's completely — yeah, maybe I'll send some people your way that are defected from the lab, worried precisely about this. Well, thank you so much, Nathan. This was a lot of fun. And yeah, I'm really excited to see what Trillium is up to now that it's finally launched.

Nathan: Yeah, thanks so much for having me.

item.description:
# 三重资本之外，被忽视的"第四种资本"：组织熵
Nathan 把模型进步归为 compute / data / talent 三种资本，但他随口提到的那句"Meta 做了一次 total reset 才重新上扬"才是整段对话最被低估的洞见。真正的瓶颈不是你拥有多少资本，而是**组织图（org chart）能否让资本有效流经**。这其实是一个被遗忘的工业史命题——贝尔实验室的衰落、Xerox PARC 把图形界面拱手让给苹果、英特尔错过移动——都不是输在钱或人，而是输在组织让这些资本"沉淀"而非"流动"。放在今天：OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的优势不在于囤了多少 H100，而在于它们是**少数几家把"重做组织架构"这件事当成常规操作而非危机手段**的公司。开源阵营真正的硬约束，可能不是算力，而是没有一个敢让 Postdoc 全员重新组队的治理结构。
# 关于蒸馏的反直觉信号：开源社区被"困在旧 Qwen"是最有力的反证
主流叙事认为中国模型靠蒸馏 Claude/GPT 快速追赶。Nathan 给出一个让人意外的反驳：**如果蒸馏真那么强，为什么完全开源的后训练复现者至今

item.title: [Lex Clips] Jensen Huang shows Lex Fridman around Taiwan (Highlight)
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、夜市作为"反摩尔定律"的朝圣地

黄仁勋带 Lex 认识台湾的第一站不是台积电、不是晶圆实验室，而是夜市——这个选择比它看起来更有深意。全世界算力密度最高的芯片都从这座岛屿流出，而黄仁勋亲自示范的"台湾灵魂"却是蚵仔煎、油烟和摊贩的即兴叫卖。这不是矛盾，而是一个被外人严重低估的互补系统：台积电 3nm 代表"极致规则驱动的秩序"，夜市代表"极致涌现驱动的秩序"。同一座岛同时精通了两种相反方向的复杂度处理方式——这或许比任何产业政策都更能解释，为什么台湾在半导体格局里几乎不可被复制。

二、"It doesn't make any sense"：遇到复杂系统的两个阶段

Lex 在短短几十秒里说了两句关键的话——先是"It blew my mind"，后来是"It doesn't make any sense"。表面上他是在评论食物，但从认知科学角度看，这恰好是人类遭遇任何高维复杂系统时必经的两个阶段：先是感官过载的敬畏，然后是语义框架失效时的困惑。有趣的巧合是，这几乎也是当下神经网络研究员谈论大模型涌现行为时最常用的两句话。黄仁勋领着 Fridman 穿过的那条夜市小巷，其实在用食物重演"面对涌现智能"的现象学教学。

三、蚵仔煎与 CUDA：一个被忽视的"边缘起源"法则（跨领域连接）

跨个领域想一下——蚵仔煎这道菜的真正起源是物资匮乏年代的"剩料整合"：没米就用地瓜粉，没肉就凑小蚵仔和零散青菜。它是一个教科书级的 bootstrap 产物。而黄仁勋真正改变世界的那条路径同样是 bootstrap：GPU 本来只是给游戏玩家画三角形的"剩余算力"，直到有人把它拿来做矩阵乘法。真正改变文明走向的技术，很少从"旗舰项目"诞生，几乎都是从边缘、剩料、玩乐里生长出来的。所以当他说自己"爱夜市爱得不能不来"——那不只是乡愁，而是一个一辈子都在"把边缘玩具变成基础设施"的人，在向自己的方法论本身致敬。令人意外的是：这位把 AI 算力推上神坛的人，向世界展示自己故乡时选的隐喻，恰好是反精英、反规划、反顶层设计的那一面。

📝 转录文本

开场 · Setting off

We're going to hang out for a couple days. I'm going to show him Taiwan.

夜市初印象 · First impressions at the night market

It blew my mind. Ladies and gentlemen, let's preach. This is the famous oyster pancake. Amaz... in the —

黄仁勋的夜市情结 · Jensen at home in the night market

Jensen loves the night market way too much not to do it. This smells delicious. Let's see what this is. Try this thing. It doesn't make any sense.

收束 · Wrap

That's a wrap on one of the most incredible weeks of my life.

观看原视频 →
